speechtext:
On the order for motions:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Acting Prime Minister): Mr. Speaker, I have now had an opportunity of investigating that grave matter of a breach of the privileges of the house about which the hon. member for Lake Centre and several newspapers have been so seriously concerned.
On Friday last the hon. member, after reading the terms of order.for return No. 258, said:
A perusal of the documents produced yesterday shows that in spite of the fact that parliament passed the order without any qualifications that any documents should be refused, a number of the letters have been deliberately omitted and the file is in the position of having been stripped and denuded of four known letters, as well as others. The four letters which do not appear in the file are the following:
(1)	A letter from Mr. Robinette, K.C., of Toronto, dated March 22, referred to in letter of March 26.
(2)	Letter from Mr. Miall to Mr. Anderson, dated the 26th of March.
(3)	Copy of letter, October 12, from Mr. Robinette, K.C., sent to Mr. MacNamara, the deputy minister.
(4)	Letter of the deputy minister of justice to Mr. MacNamara, dated the 19th of October, 1945.
These four letters are referred to in the correspondence produced, but have not been produced.
When the hon. member made that statement I felt, as I am sure all hon. members who heard it must have felt, that it must be serious or no hon. member would be making it. On examining the file this is what it reveals: two of the letters which were alleged to have been deliberately omitted, of which the file had been "stripped and denuded", which, according to the statement, do not appear on the file, are there and were there all the time. One of them is the letter from Mr. Miall to Mr. Anderson dated the 26th of March; it is document 4 of the file,; another is the letter of the Deputy Minister of Justice to Mr. MacNamara dated the 19th of October, 1945; it is No. 6 on the file. The other two documents, being letters from Mr. Robinette to the Department of Justice dated, one, March 22 and the other October 12, are, as I explained yesterday, not letters from one department to another-which were the only things called for in the order-but letters written to the

Privilege-Mr. Diejenbaker
Department of Justice by a lawyer acting as such for the department and which, according to the invariable rule, are not produced in parliament. Now, if there has been any "affront to parliament and to the privileges of parliament", it would seem to be only in the fact that the hon. member has once again allowed his zeal about cases which he calls cases having "odoriferous characteristics" to outrun his discretion and has made, quite inadvertently I am sure but nevertheless without sufficient care, positive statements to this house about a document which on its face shows that the statements are just not true.

Mr. DIEFENBAKER.: He may laugh and hon. members may jeer. But to-day, when we speak so much of lawlessness in the land, lawlessness on the part of the government is as serious as lawlessness anywhere else.
Here is the record. In the first place, sir, I asked the question:
Have any criminal proceedings been taken or are any contemplated in connection with an
alleged conspiracy arising out of the improper use of army rejection or medical discharges at Camp Borden since 1943?
The answer is no. The next question was:
Was the matter investigated by the R.C.M.P. and did they recommend prosecution?
Here is the answer:
The R.C.M.P. investigated and reported, which report was reviewed by counsel who was acting as agent for the crown in a prosecution case having to do with mobilization regulations. Counsel expressed the opinion that a review should be made by another counsel although he was also of the opinion that the reports indicated a prima facie case.
Counsel in question was Mr. Robinette, K.C., who I am informed was counsel for the prosecution in the case of one Lennox, on March 22, 1945, at the city of Hamilton, Lennox having been charged with having passed one of these fake medical certificates, and he gave evidence there that he paid one Joseph Bagley at the Humber Hotel in Toronto $1,200 for the certificate. He was charged with uttering a false document and received three months. My information is that Mr. Robinette, K.C., an outstanding counsel, set forth the facts and indicated that there was a prima facie case and then another counsel was brought in. What his report was it is not for me to say, but my information is that it too advised that there was a prima facie case.
Now we go on with the record. As far as the Department of Justice is concerned, Mr. Varcoe, the deputy minister, made sure that tlie responsibility did not rest on that department. Here is the correspondence from the beginning. The first letter is dated October 19, 1945:

Mr. Speaker, may I continue to put the record before the house? Here is a letter dated November 13, 1945:
Mr. F. P. Varcoe,
Deputy Minister of Justice,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Varcoe:
With reference to your letter of October 19th relative to prosecutions of Brother Arnold and Major J. A. Elliott of Toronto.
I would recommend that this file he put away for three or four months and then the matter could be reviewed.
I am sure that I will receive the endorsation from the minister for this proposal.
Very truly yours,
(Sgd.) A. MacNamara.
After it has been put away for two or three months a letter is written by Mr. Varcoe a little later in which he sets forth the following on April 10. Your Honour will have noticed that the cooling off period had elapsed:
April 10, 1946.
Dear Mr. MacNamara:
May I have a reply to my letter of March 16, with reference to Brother Arnold and Major J. A. Elliott.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) F. P. Varcoe,
Deputy Minister.
Finally on April 16, 1946 Mr. MacNamara wrote to Mr. Varcoe, the deputy minister of justice, as follows:

Dear Mr. Varcoe:
I have your letter of April 10th, File No. 146298 and I would recommend that this file be closed and that prosecution be not proceeded with.
Now there is the record; the omission of counsel's letter from the file, which was part and parcel of the file that should have been brought before parliament; the omission of all the other letters to which I have already referred. First you have the prosecution of Lennox in 1945; you have evidence there given, and you have the report of Mr. Robinette, K.C.; you have the report of counsel, as admitted by the government in its answer, that a prima facie case had been made out; then you have the deputy minister of labour advising the Department of Justice, first, that they allow the matter to remain for three or four months, and finally that there be no prosecution.
I say, sir, the record speaks for itself and the record establishes everything I said. What is more, the rights of parliament are still being flouted by the refusal of the government to produce the entire file in this case which, if produced, will reveal interference with the administration of justice, which ought not to be condoned in this house.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to move, seconded by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling):
That the said bill be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole for the purpose of reconsidering subsection 3 of paragraph 3, and subsection 9 of section 13 of paragraph 4 thereof.
It is not my purpose to occupy the time of the house for more than a very few minutes. I simply wish to put ourselves on record as being opposed to the manner in which this measure as it affects cooperatives has been handled from the beginning, and to the form in which it is now found with respect to the taxation of cooperatives. If it was the law prior to the introduction of this measure that cooperatives should be taxed, and if the law was right, it should have been enforced. If the law was wrong, it should have been changed. But the government refused to take either position. It is leaving the impression with the private trade that it is going to tax cooperatives, and it is leaving the impression with the cooperatives that they can so handle their affairs that they will not be taxed at all. The government is simply trying to play both ends against the middle. The net result will be, if this measure is passed in its present form, that cooperatives will be turned into investment enterprises.
The three renjaining objections I have to this bill I shall deal with very briefly. Some of the objections the government has already agreed to have removed, but I should like to refer to three remaining objections.
The first objection is to subsection 3 of paragraph 3, which I suggest with all deference is discriminatory. It provides that new cooperative organizations will be exempt from taxation for three years if they organize after January 1 next; but it does not provide for any exemptions for new organizations formed prior to that time but not yet three years old. I say that this is a discrimination against new cooperatives. If it is a good policy to apply

Income War Tax
Mr. Speaker, I am not going to spend a long time dealing with this matter this morning.
Hear, hear!

I hear cries of "hear, hear" but I do not mind that. I would not take any time at all if I did not consider it a very necessary duty in the interests of the .people of this country. Before saying what I had planned to say may I just remark in passing that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken), occupying the position he does, being closer to the Speaker, and wearing a light coloured suit of clothes, caught the eye of Mr. Speaker before I did; otherwise I would have moved an amendment similar to the one he has moved. However, we shall take a little different attitude than that taken pro 'ously by the Progressive Conservative party; we shall support his motion, though the other day, when we had a similar motion up for discussion, they did not support us. I want to remind the leader of the opposition that everything he said here this morning is about

Income War Tax
a month and ten days late, because I set out the whole position in my budget speech on July 10.
I regret- very much that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is not in his place this morning. When he was speaking the other day he took a tremendous amount of credit to the Liberal party for the growth of cooperatives. At page 4724 of Hansard, when this matter was under discussion, in the last paragraph of his remarks he said:
All I wish to say now is that the whole record indicates that the real founders of the cooperative movement in the Dominion of Canada were the members of the Liberal party. Their policies have been behind the cooperative movement; they are still behind it, and when this legislation gets through it will have the support of the very people who my friends of the C.C.F. party are trying to lead us to believe are opposed to it in the province of Saskatchewan.
Since this matter has been under consideration, and particularly since the minister made that speech, I have had many letters from people in the province of Saskatchewan concerned with the cooperative movement, but none of those letters bear out the minister's statement that they support this action. The minister took occasion to refer to a gentleman who was very highly regarded in the province of Saskatchewan, Hon. W. R. Motherwell, and I heartily endorse every personal tribute he paid to that notable gentleman of the prairies. The members of this party take second place to no one in honouring and paying tribute to Bill Motherwell; everybody in Saskatchewan who follows things will do that. He was a grand old rebel, and in the front line of the farm forces all the time in the early days of the century, and -he always had the interests of the farmers and cooperatives at heart. If he -had any fault at all it was his loyal belief that his hopes could be realized through the Liberal party, and he tried to move that party in this direction. Because of his personal ability he achieved a remarkable degree of success, and we honour him for that. His successor, however, cannot lay claim to any such achievement. He has had to be pushed into every progressive movement ever undertaken in our province, and only the fear of the loss of votes ever made him take a stand in support of the progressive movement. So when he takes to the Liberal party credit for building up cooperatives he is far from the facts. The cooperative movement in Saskatchewan was built by the people of Saskatchewan, of all shades of political opinion. It is open to all people, of both sexes, of all colours, all races, all creeds. Those are the people who 63260-320J
built it. Hundreds of them went out on horseback and on foot in the early days in support of these cooperatives.
If the Minister of Agriculture had been correct in his statement it never would have been necessary to remove the Liberal party from power in Saskatchewan. I want to give the house a little history in regard to the record of the Liberal party with regard to cooperatives in that province. A very close personal friend of mine, my seat mate, the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Burton), sat in the Saskatchewan legislature from 1938 to 1943, during which time he served on the public accounts committee. During that time the public accounts showed that the provincial government purchased large quantities of petroleum products for their power commission and other government departments, but not a dollar's worth during that five-year period was bought from the consumers' cooperative refinery in Regina, right at the seat of government. Nor did the Liberal government during that period give any business to any cooperative enterprise in the province except in those few cases where farmers who were on relief took their meagre relief slips and spent them at cooperative stores. Practically no government printing was given to what was at that time the only cooperative owned newspaper of that province, the Western Producer, owned by the Saskatchewan wheat pool. In fact their whole record has been one of lip service, with absolutely no record of active, good support.
The bill before us for third reading is a vindication of what I have said previously in this debate and what I am saying now. I have said before, and I say again, the introduction of the provision compelling a cooperative to show a three per cent profit before it can pay dividends and so on is in itself a clear indication of the antagonism of the Liberal party toward the building up of this great cooperative movement. Had it been my good fortune to catch your eye first, Mr. Speaker, I was going to move that this bill be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole with instructions that it have power to reconsider the provisions already set out in the amendment of the leader of the opposition, and also those having to do with the three per cent tax on cooperatives. As I have said already, our group are going to follow a different line from that of the Progressive Conservatives or of the Liberals. We are not only going to give lip service; we are going to support the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition, as we would have
Income War Tax

hoped-rather faintly-that perhaps some of them might have stayed in the house and voted for our amendment had we been able to move it.

Mr. Speaker, during the discussion which has taken place on this matter I have sat quietly in this chamber and said nothing. In the county of Charlotte, as I have tried to point out in this house, we have a big fishing industry. During the past five or six years all those fishermen have paid income tax. By way of comparison let me say that in that county, with its population of 25,000 people, the fishermen have paid more income tax in the last six years than have all the farmers in the province of New Brunswick.
In my county there are four or five owners for each sardine fishing right. There is no reason in the world why those fishermen could not form a cooperative and clear themselves from paying income tax, like the farmers in western Canada are trying to do. I believe in fairness; and if one group in the country is going to be compelled to pay income tax- and I have every respect in the world for hon. members who will rise in their places and look after the interests of their constituents-other groups should pay also. There are hon. members in the house who would tax one class of primary producers although excluding another, and in my view that is most unfair. I believe that if every hon. member votes according to his principles he would1 vote to tax all the primary producers in Canada on exactly the same basis.

Mr. Speaker, we have held the view throughout that the budget legislation dealing with cooperatives was detrimental to the growth of a movement to which thousands of people in this country have devoted a great deal of time and attention, and which they have endeavoured to 'build up to meet their own needs.
On July 8 we moved a subamendment to the amendment moved by the official opposition. The official opposition of course had already moved its amendment, and in it there was no criticism of the taxation of cooperatives. May I point out that in our subamendment we said:
That the budget fails in its tax proposals to recognize the principle that cooperatives are non-profit-making organizations.
I have been unable to understand why, at a late date, the official opposition suddenly picked up this view, a view they had officially opposed by voting against it. My experience throughout the years, when this has been

under discussion, has been that Mr. Thorvald-son, president of the Income Tax Payers Association, so called, who was responsible for the circulation of thousands of cards in this country, and also the only Progressive Conservative member from the city of Winnipeg who sits in the Manitoba legislature, represents the point of view of the party rather than the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Bracken).
However, I am glad indeed to have an opportunity of voting for reference back to the committee this morning, because that is precisely what we had intended to do had the amendment not been moved first.
I do say this, in the interests of open, free and frank discussion, that hon. members who sit in the house-on all sides of the house- who have expressed disagreement with the position we take regarding the taxation of cooperatives, should rise and express their opinions so that the country may know exactly where they stand in this matter.
I think this proposal transcends party issues; we have said that throughout. It so happens that this party, in common with others, and in common with other people in various parts of Canada, takes the view that these, nonprofit organizations should neither be taxed nor compelled, as the leader of the opposition has said, to operate as investment corporations.
To my mind, apart altogether from any other provision of the bill, the proposal to compel cooperatives to compute interest of three per cent on the capital employed strikes at the very roots of cooperative philosophy, cooperative thought and cooperative endeavour.
I shall not prolong the discussion, because I believe this matter has been thoroughly discussed, and little more could be added to it. I do say, however, as leader of this party, that we intend to support the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition.
Mr. SOLON E. LOW ({Peace River): Mr. Speaker, I would say just a word on behalf of the Social Credit group respecting the amendment offered by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken). I am not at all interested in the fight for place that seems to be going on between the two parties sitting to my right. It does not matter to me who receives the credit-
Or to me.

-for the moving of this amendment. I find however that this group is favourable to the amendment proposed this morning. Because of the fundamental differ-

Income War Tax
enees between cooperatives and corporations it is our opinion that, with justice and equity, cooperatives simply cannot be placed in the same category as corporations for taxation purposes.
We are definitely opposed to anything which would be prejudicial to the growth and continuation of cooperatives as a vital force in the Canadian economy. We believe the bill as it now stands before the house for third reading is prejudicial to that growth and continuation. We reiterate the recommendation offered some days ago by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) when he spoke for the Social Credit group in this house. Perhaps I might outline quickly what he said. In the first place we hold that the government should withdraw the bill as it applies to cooperatives, and should concern itself for the next year with the drafting of a new cooperatives act, which act should carefully define what is meant by a true cooperative. In that act it should be made definitely clear that the wheat pools would not be required to pay income tax retroactively. The act should also lay down the conditions which in fairness and equity would make possible the continuation in the future of true cooperatives as a vital organization or group of organizations in the Canadian economy.
Because of the failure of the present bill to do those things, the Social Credit group will support the amendment proposed by the leader of the opposition.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry I did not hear clearly what was said by the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bentley), but from what I did hear it would seem that he was saying something that has become familiar to those of us in Saskatchewan-that the great friend of the cooperatives is the C.C.F. party. That has been said over and over again, and anyone who has lived in Saskatchewan for any length of time knows that it is an attempt to put something across on the people of Saskatchewan and the people of Canada. Our people know, for example, that long before the C.C.F. was ever heard of, Saskatchewan was noted for its support-particularly under the Liberal party-of the cooperative movement. They know that long before the C.C.F. was ever heard or thought of, one of the greatest cooperatives in the whole world, the Saskatchewan Cooperative Elevator Company, had had its beginning. They know that the Liberal party set up a branch of one of its departments of government for the purpose of promoting, developing, supporting and encouraging cooperatives.
We have been deluged with the suggestion that the present government in Saskatchewan is the first one in that province to have a department of government directly concerned with the development and promotion of cooperatives. Of course everybody in Saskatchewan laughs at that suggestion because the present deputy minister, Mr. Arnason, has just been given another title. Previously he was in charge of a department which had to do with the development of cooperatives, a branch of another department. But by changing the name and making him a deputy minister, by actually appointing a man to be minister of cooperatives, they tried to put the idea across that they are the first people who have actually intervened in the promotion and development of cooperatives. Every C.C.F. member in this house knows that for many years we had a branch of government under Mr. Arnason, the present deputy minister.
How large a staff?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
How large a staff? We do not judge the effectiveness of our work by talking about tlhe large number of civil servants drawn from all over the world who are there. Perhaps that is the idea of the C.C.F., and it looks like it. Consider the number of experts they have imported from all over the world. It looks as though they had no confidence in the home grown product; in fact I have heard them boasting about the number of people they have brought in from the outside.
I want to say, and I say this after some study of the development of political affairs, that any movement which feels itself constrained in order to develop itself to base its development upon fallacies, upon partial statements of fact, upon half truths, is bound to be found out in the long run. I want to tell hon. members that that is actually happening to-day in Saskatchewan. Mr. Arnason, the present deputy minister of cooperatives, has been an employee of the Saskatchewan government for at least the last ten or fifteen years.
As what?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
As director of cooperatives. He is doing exactly the same, work now as he did ten years ago under the Liberal government. There has been no real change of principle in regard to government support and help. The Saskatchewan government supported and helped cooperatives. In that regard there has been nothing but misrepresentation of the facts. That cannot be denied, and every hon. member knows it. They know also that public moneys are being spent by

I do not know what was in the mind of the gentleman who said, "For God's sake read your contract", but I do know that that same man was the man who was placed in charge of the Saskatchewan Cooperative Elevator Company and who brought it from small beginnings to the place where it became one of the greatest farmer-owned and cooperatively-controlled grain handling institutions in the whole world.

speechtext: Don't worry; I do not belong to them and I never did. That was the beginning of the C. C. F. party. speechtext: There was this new organization-I know hon. members hate to hear this, because it must bring back searchings of conscience to any people who are conscientious about such things. I say this to hon. members opposite that when they fight and work to get the support of reformers, of people who believe in the reform of our present system, in order to put into power people who believe in socialism and want to destroy the present system by taking over all the means of wealth production, they are preaching something which is fundamentally false.
Who is the hon. member talking about?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I am talking about the C.C.F. The hon. member understands only too well. Come over here.

Once you go far enough along the lines of socialism, along the line of bringing in state control of the means of wealth production and of the ownership of the natural resources of the country, you have got to the point where the government is so all-powerful that there is no possible distinction between it and a communist dictatorship.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Come on, answer the question.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Once your government owns the means of wealth production, once it owns the assets of the country, I defy any C.C.F.'er to tell me the difference between that and communism.
Get up and tell us.

speechtext: That is why I say that the C.C.F. is the way-maker for communism.

speechtext: Then why not encourage cooperatives?

Mr. Speaker, we have a very fine spectacle in this house to-day. The Progressive Conservative party, which has always been the friend and the supporter of private enterprise, to-day takes up the cudgels on behalf of the cooperatives. The anomaly is not so great as it would appear at first sight, because if we consider some powerful organizations from the west, especially the wheat pools, we are less surprised. I rise in defence of the Liberal party's policy in this respect. I do so with the conviction that bill No. 368 which is now before this house, can on the whole in no way harm the cooperative movement in Canada and particularly in the province of Quebec.
I am a supporter of the cooperatives. I was brought up in that movement and it is a source of deep satisfaction to me to recall that, as early as 1908, my father, Notary Belzile, of Rimouski, established the second credit union in the province of Quebec.
I shall not go so far as to say that the cooperative idea is a religion to me, but it is certainly part of my economic and political creed. I have studied the cooperative movement for a long time, and I have realized how beneficial it can be to our province and to the country at large. Therefore, when the resolution was first introduced in this house, I made it a point to study it most carefully.
The matter gives rise to much controversy. Some people are in favour of the taxation of cooperatives; others hold an opposite view. Mr. Speaker, before the one o'clock recess, I explained that the government, in reply to the representations that had been made to them in connection with the taxation of cooperatives, had appointed a commission. I gave the names of the members of that body. However, I wish to emphasize the personality of Mr. Amason. He is an expert on the cooperative movement, and is well qualified to propound its ideas and aspirations. He is at this time deputy minister of the cooperation department in the C.C.F. government of Saskatchewan. The commission has conducted an inquiry throughout the country. It has had a great number of public sittings. Many briefs-more than 175, I believe-were submitted for its consideration. After sitting in many places from Vancouver to Halifax, three of its .members have even made a trip to England in order to make a survey of the cooperative movement in that country. They have -met British experts in London, Liverpool and Manchester. The object of that trip to England was to ascertain the effect of taxation on the cooperative movement there. As everyone knows cooperatives are taxed in. England. In September, 1945, the commission submitted its report. It was unanimous, which is rather surprising, if we consider the opinion of the various members, and the fact that their occupations were quite dissimilar. Its recommendation was to the effect that cooperatives should be taxed. It stated as follows:
We are of the opinion there is no general class or group of cooperative associations in Canada to-day whose income should be declared not to be liable to taxation .'. .
That was the unanimous opinion of the commission. The situation which the commission had to investigate was this. In 1930 the Income War Tax Act was amended by the insertion of section (4) (p), whereby cooperatives were exempted from the income tax. According to a quite authoritative legal construction that provision did not imply complete exemption. Under that interpretation of the clause, the cooperatives could be taxed. As a result, some important western organizations have been advised that they would have to pay income tax. The cooperatives who were so advised have disputed the construction placed on section 4 (p) and they have brought the matter before the courts, where it is still pending. In view of that imbroglio, the commission deemed it necessary that section 4 (p) be repealed and it made in its report a recommendation along that line that was also unanimous. It stated:
As a result of the ambiguities of language and the difficulty of administering the section, we are of the opinion that the section, in its present form, cannot survive the attacks made upon it. In suggesting its repeal, we do so in the consciousness that enterprises which are truly cooperative in organization and operation, have no need of the exceptive provisions thereof. If they make no profit they are not taxable. Those associations which do not so qualify, should not be accorded a blanket exemption to which they are not otherwise entitled.
That was the unanimous report of the Commission and even Mr. Arnason endorsed that principle. Consequently, the Government has proposed the repeal of section 4(p). Before that recommendation, the position was this: under that interpretation of the act, the cooperatives were liable to the income tax- they have been so taxable since 1931. No prescription can be invoked against the government. A claim for taxes does not lapse in favour of the rate-payer. That is a well known law .principle. Therefore, in. opposition to the representations made by the cooperatives, the government deemed it necessary to make the latter liable to taxation, and I think they were right. The principle underlying taxation .is that equal treatment should be meted out to all taxpayers. Under no circumstances can there be any discrimination' as between the various taxpayers. If it is admitted, as the commission did admit, that some of the operations conducted by cooperatives are of a purely commercial nature, and that they compete directly with private concerns, it is obvious that .the exemption of cooperatives from taxation would mean a discrimination, and under certain circumstances, an injustice which could not but give rise to discontent. Under the provisions of the provincial laws that apply to cooperatives, the latter are corporations and their members or shareholders are responsible only for the unpaid amount of their subscriptions or shares. The corporation is a person as distinct from the individuals who belong to it. Under the law, the establishment of a cooperative creates a legal entity that is new and distinct from its promoters; it has rights and obligations different from those of its members. It is "a person" as defined in the Income War Tax Act. Its members only have a limited responsibility, which places them on a par with the shareholders of a company. In its operations, the cooperative resorts to the usual business methods; if its operations bring no surplus the cooperative has no income and therefore is not taxable.. But if its operations show a surplus, it is an income within the meaning of the law, and that .income is therefore

Income War Tax
taxable. We have to consider where the income ultimately goes; it is a matter of distribution or non-distribution. If the income is distributed, it becomes an income for the shareholder who receives it, and as such it is liable to taxation in the hands of that shareholder. If the income is not distributed; if on the contrary, it is put, by some method or other, into the capital of the cooperative, such action on the part of the board of directors does not change the nature of the income. Consequently, it remains taxable, but in this instance, in the hands of the cooperative. If, out of the income of a taxpayer an amount is put into some kind of fund and that amount is said not to be taxable, this constitutes an inequality as regards the rate-payer and, of course, in the case of all the taxpayers in this country. Such is, in essence, the principle underlying the taxation of cooperatives, and I think it is fair.
To sum up my argument, I may say that the cooperatives are organizations whose immediate object is the elimination of middlemen's profits.
No one will gainsay this statement of principle. Therefore, they operate in order to realize these profits for themselves; and the commission is very clear on that point. Then the cooperatives must pay the tax on the same grounds as the middleman with whom they compete,-if they have profits, of course. To exempt them would be a discrimination in their favour, as far as the law is concerned. Such an exemption would be of no particular advantage to the public at large and its burden would fall proportionately on the rest of the taxpayers, which would give rise to dissatisfaction; as I said a while back, it would be unfair.
In order to implement the McDougall commission recommendations, the government has submitted, with the budget, a certain number of resolutions. These resolutions, as is now generally known, relate to three different subjects. They exempt credit unions, but bring mutual fire, life and accident insurance companies under taxation, except church mutual associations. As for ordinary cooperatives, the commission declared that those that were making profits had to pay the tax, while those that did not were exempt.
These resolutions have given rise to numerous representations from the cooperatives of the province of Quebec.
A large number of representations were submitted to me from supporters of taxation, on the one hand, who pointed out that the government was most generous towards the cooperative movement, in fact, too magnanimous in their opinion. Other representations were put forward by cooperatives complaining of the treatment meted out to them. The problem thus put on a dual aspect, and the two opponents assailed the recommendations of the commission which were incorporated in the budget resolutions.
As I said a while ago, I am in favour of cooperatives. Indeed, a group of members from rural districts submitted representations to the government. We explained that equal distribution of patronage dividends to members and non-members alike might foil the development of the cooperative movement. In fact, since one need no longer be a member of these organizations, that is, need run no risks and assume no responsibilities to draw patronage dividends, non-members would no longer hav* any incentive to join such an enterprise. These representations, put forward by the cooperatives of my province, were justified. We submitted them to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) and to the officers of his department, and they understood our grievances. We also pointed out to the government that the six months delay set for the payment of patronage dividends was too short. In fact, some of our cooperatives, and more especially the creameries and others whose activities are of a rather seasonal character, need most of their funds in the spring. We pointed out, therefore, that under the circumstances, a twelve months period was essential. Here again the government agreed to our representations.
As to cash payments, no more than a method of administration is involved. The cooperative need only, in some way or other, credit the shareholder with the patronage dividend to benefit from an exemption for said amount on which, as I said a while ago, the shareholder will be taxed. The statement of the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) was based on these representations.
Therefore, since.the government has agreed to our proposals. I deem it my duty to support this bill. By means of this bill, and as a result of the amendments allowed, our claims are satisfied in full. It fully meets the requirements of cooperatives. Not only will it cause them no harm, but I would go so far as to say that it will help them, and foster their further development.
The present debate is probably-and even unquestionably-the greatest propaganda ever put forward in Canada in favour of the cooperative movement. It is my hope, there-
Income War Tax

fore, that our cooperatives will appreciate the value of their movement and the advantages of communal endeavour.
But what remains of those resolutions? There remains the very object of the two amendments now under consideration: the three-year exemption clause and the one commonly described as the 3 per cent clause.
As regards the three-year clause, whose removal is sought in order to make the exemption retroactive over three years, its suppression would be unfair. There is no provision for the retroactive application of a legal measure. Legally the proposition is quite unsound. You cannot go back and exempt an organization that might have been liable to taxation.
As for the 3 per cent clause, it has been woefully misconstrued. In a generally well-informed newspaper, I have read, under the by-line of an alert financial editor, an interpretation that was quite wrong. This is what it said:
The government wants to put a three per cent tax on cooperatives' employed capital. The application of such a measure would be comparable to taxing a farmer on the value of his chattels.
This interpretation is quite erroneous. This is not a tax on capital; it is a tax on income. It is the Income War Tax Act we are dealing with here. The 3 per cent clause is merely a basis, a schedule of taxation. We say to the cooperatives:	"You are using a certain
amount of capital for the purposes of your business. If you make a profit-there is no commercial profit without capital-and if this profit is greater than 3 per cent of the capital employed, you must pay income tax on your real profit. If your profit is less than 3 per cent, you are left with some income at least, with a real profit subject to taxation. Here is how the rule applies:	you may not
reduce an income of 10 per cent to less than 3 per cent by subtracting depreciation allowances, by distributing patronage dividends or by paying interest rates. If you bring it down to less than 3 per cent, you will be taxed on the basis of 3 per cent. In other words, if a cooperative tries to reduce an income of $1,000 to less than $300 by means of deductions, patronage dividends, interest payments and depreciation allowances, it will be taxed on the sum of $300 at the current rate. It will pay 30 per cent of $300; or $90, which is far from 3 per cent of the capital.
All in all, I believe that the cooperatives will benefit by the enactment of the present legislation. It will force them to make statutory reserves under provincial laws, to put aside certain taxable funds derived from their
fMr. Belzile.]
business profits.
I am convinced that the implementation of the act will not prove detrimental to cooperatives but will compel them to set aside reserves, thus permitting them to redeem their total debt within a period of ten or fifteen years.
The passing of this measure will lead to the establishment of a standard system of operations in all cooperatives. In such a vast country as ours, laws vary from one province to another and their terms are not uniform. As a result, operations are conducted on a different basis in various cooperatives. They will immediately profit by the adoption of a standard system. I humbly submit that, in view of the situation, the amendment introduced by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) should be rejected.

Mr. MAURICE LALONDE' (Labelle) moved:
_ That the second report of the committee on industrial relations, presented to the house on Saturday, August 17, 1946, be now concurred in.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in order to restore the house to its usual state of complacency may I say that I rise to support the motion of the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Lalonde). Inasmuch as I had something to do with the beginning of this committee, or at least having it set up, I assure the house, as I did then, that I intend to consider the matter objectively and without heat.
I hope that you, sir, and the house, will see the distinction between my method of approach and that which we saw this morning. What happened this morning reminded me of
fMr. Gillis.l
the churches we used to have in western Canada, where a boy would pump wind into the pipe organ to make it go. I was one of those boys; we worked in relays. This morning I heard an organ playing with all the stops pulled out and there were at least two boys applying the wind. I trust that I shall not fall into that position this afternoon.
I cannot begin without complimenting and commending our chairman. I realize that it is not a compliment to a chairman of a committee to congratulate him upon his impartiality-the chairmen of all committees in this house surely must be impartial-but I do want to compliment him upon the way in which he administered' that impartiality, creating a basis of action which reached a new high both in dignity and' generally in the conduct of the proceedings of a committee.
I should like to say something about my fellow members on that committee. My experience in the House of Commons is limited to two sessions, the one which has gone and this one which, let us hope, is passing. Having sat on a number of committees, this was a new experience to me. I think all the thirty-five of us who were there were deeply impressed by the seriousness of the situation-except for the odd momentary outburst which was confined to the first two days in our forty-nine sessions, and we had that many. There was no sign of anyone seeking political advantage. They were a bunch of grand1 men trying to do something for their country.
In saying this I must also include the members of the press gallery who so fairly and fully reported this matter across Canada. But in saying that to them I stop short of the editorial chairs of the papers of this country. I say about those people, some of them only of course, that I do not envy them their position sitting on their air-cushioned seats in their ivory towers continuing this twofingered clacking on a typewriter which has lulled them into such a sense of somnolence that they cannot stand the accouchement of a new idea. It is very easy in that position to be always criticizing, but they have been unable to give birth to any new ideas. We have found that throughout the course of the sittings of this committee in some of the newspapers in this country.
I intend to deal briefly with this question of industrial unrest, and in doing so I go away back to the time perhaps when a member of the tribe from rocks and wood fashioned the first instrument of destruction. The creation of the first knife was by an individual for the chief. That was because of industrial unrest, a seeking to get along. We have that

Industrial Relations
now, and I hope we always will have industrial unrest, because therein lies ambition and therein lies improvement. The maker of a mousetrap seeks to make a better mousetrap, and the -man who does the work seeks always a larger portion of that dollar which is brought forth by the mousetrap once it reaches the consuming public.
I am anxious to make a clear distinction between industrial unrest and industrial chaos, because that is the position this country is in at the present time. Perhaps here it might be advisable for me to tell the house of a message I have just received. It is supposed to be a Canadian Press message put out about fifteen minutes ago. It indicates that the gates at the steel plant at Hamilton have been opened and that traffic is moving freely back and forth into and out of that plant.

speechtext:
I shall read this. It reads:
After first paragraph saying picket line open on authority Stelco, Canadian Press then on own authority says (in paraphrase).
Autos filled with Stelco employees passed through gates escorted by city police.
At least ten ears filled with employees entered the plant.	.
"We want to stop them, but what can we do?" a picket captain was quoted. The constables told us they have a legal right to go in and out of the plant.
A meeting of union executives was called at the main gate to decide the next move.
A thirty-year employee of Stelco is quoted by Canadian Press as saying that 900 men have telephoned Stelco officials to ask that they be given work.
The growth of the labour movement in the civilized world has been an amazing growth. It has been a splendid growth and, broadly speaking, it has been a very proper growth. But as we know, in all growth sometimes we find a canker, and attached to labour-I do not want to be criticized until I finish this sentence-at the present moment is the canker of communism. I say that that is no part of the labour movement; it is a political movement boring into labour movement, seeking by the instillation of fear, by the preaching of false doctrine, with the ultimate goal of a general strike, to grasp and hold completely political and executive authority in the Dominion of Canada. That is admittedly the end sought by the communist party in this country.
The mere fact that they have sought to go where there are masses of men is not a criticism of those men and the labour movement. It is something which they themselves-on
our committee I know there were two men holding union cards, and they were not in my party-are fighting, and have been fighting- there are three individuals because I am looking at another one-in a constant battle against that subversive political movement. It is unfortunate that they have made some progress, but I say that the heart of the labour movement is still sound. It beats with a rhythm both healthy and patriotic. It seeks for itself, and it justly seeks its proper place in our Canadian economy. The action of labour-there were a few blow-offs here and there-throughout the whole war was complete proof of what I have just said, and of the basic soundness of labour in this country. There were excesses, but I am quite sure that there always will be. We must remember when we speak of excesses in the actions of labour that they are no greater and no more than those that occur in other segments of our Canadian economy. I do not care whether you come from agriculture, from the dairy men, from the stock men, from the owners or from the manufacturers, it does not do for you just to speak of one segment of our economy and say: You are blameworthy because you have gone to excesses in the normal conduct of your business.
I must say that I was greatly impressed by one remark made by Mr. Pat Conroy when he was giving evidence during the sittings of the committee. I think I have him accurately, and he said this: "It is plain that aside from this continent all the rest of the world has gone or is going either socialistic or communistic." It seems to me that that is a thought which we in this House of Commons and in this dominion may well ponder. If you look over the map of Europe, if you look over the map of Asia, what Pat Conroy said, gentlemen, you will find is true. Therefore it behooves us here, if we are to continue our way of life-I do not like ordinary expressions, but there is no better one than that-if we are to continue our methods of doing business, to look- beyond our immediate business and the colour of the ink at the end of the year in our ledgers, and realize that we have three important interests in this country-the employer, the employed and the consumer, and unless we can find a place where they shall be satisfied, then indeed are we in danger of wrecking all that we so long have held so dear.
Now what of labour organizations? It began of course with the craft unions, and those unions generally speaking were gathered together under the American Federation of Labour. Then we had the Committee of Industrial Organization: you remember that it was set up by Mr. Lewis, and then Phil
Industrial Relations

Murray took over from him, then they quarrelled, and now Mr. Lewis and his coal miners are back with the American Federation of Labour. But the thing was new. It was not an organization of labour by craft; it was an organization of labour by industry. In that it was comparatively new, and with that new method of organization new and sometimes reprehensible methods were adopted. We are fortunate indeed that until very recently we in Canada have been free from such methods. But it must be remembered that these unions are new unions. They are having or they will have their growing pains. That of course is obvious. It is also true that they are largely composed of and certainly led by younger men without much experience ini the labour movement. The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) explained that situation very well and very clearly to us in our com? mittee. So, growing so quickly, troubles have developed.
On the other side of the picture, what is the position of capital? I make this simple statement to you, that if capital had always been fair to labour there would be no need for the organization of labour. That is a very simple statement which I defy anyone to contradict. Even in recent years what has happened? The market falls off, and men are laid off by the thousands. It is all right to talk about high hourly pay, but if the work is not there so that at the end of the year.a man may add up those hours when he did work to provide a decent- living for his wife and his family, the talk of high hourly pay is complete nonsense in the budget and in the kitchen of that man and his family. It is all right to say that employment is seasonal, but what has been going on? Take your motor car industry: it does not need to be nearly as seasonal as it is. What happens? The men are out of work and the municipalities are called upon to help them; municipalities in Canada-rarely, it is true-have been paying them when a little different organization in that industry would have had the industry doing the paying for the twelve months, as of course it should.
I opened this matter some weeks ago in a speech which I made to this house. I am going to make a political remark about that speech -and this remark is not picking on anybody, which is unusual in a political remark. But I am just a little bit annoyed at being told, particularly by newspapers that are supposed to be on my own side, that this fellow Smith took a wildcat off the knees of the Prime Minister, or words to that effect. The point I have in my mind is that I am sorry that anyone should think I was quite so dumb. I assure you, Mr.. Speaker, and all hon. mem-

bers, that what I did on that occasion was done after discussion with my chief and after a caucus of this party-why? Because we felt- and it was a unanimous caucus-that the time had come when we dare not play politics, when we had to be Canadians and do what we could in the present desperate situation. If any of you think it is not desperate I commend to you the letter written by Mr. Donald Gordon to either the minister or the deputy minister of labour; if that does not give any man in this room pause, I do not know what will give him pause-whatever "pause" may be. But I mean that it will impress upon him the seriousness of the situation in which we find ourselves at the present time.
On that occasion, the house may remember, a controller had been appointed. And now, having mentioned the word "controller", I want to refer to an article in the Toronto Star of to-day. The heading is:
Kilbouni would examine every striker secretly.
After giving a recital of this sort of thing the statement continues-I am only reading a bit of it:
However, if it is put up to him, he said he believed his first step would be to find out the facts of the situation. He said he thought this could only be done by a thorough examination into the desires of the workers. He said he believed this could be done only by having all workers in the affected plants answer a set of questions.
The survey, he said, would be conducted as balloting in an election is conducted, in complete privacy. The worker would go into a booth and write his -answers and the sheet, which would bear no method of identifying the worker, would be deposited in a ballot box.
He said the survey, if it were held, should be made by entirely impartial people, with even the government eliminated. He suggested young lawyers or a firm of accountants whose impartiality would tbs beyond question should be employed.
If that is a correct statement of the methods to be adopted by this controller, he could not do that in less than nine months, with fourteen thousand men concerned. If that is the method to be adopted-and I have nothing more than the newspaper statement, the correspondent being Mr. Robert Taylor-if he has nothing more than that, it is time we had a new controller appointed in the steel industry. This of course, as everybody realizes, is just a lot of nonsense.
Now I pass on to this. First, I am anxious to compliment the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on the speed with which he acted; because you will remember it was in the afternoon that I made the suggestion for reference to a committee, and the committee was set up and met that evening. I do not

Industrial Relations
not need to read again to this house the terms of reference. They were to inquire into industrial unrest, and this committee of j'ours realized that we were not specially commissioned to settle the steel strike. What we did was this. There it was in an acute form. We were not greatly concerned with any limitation you had put upon us, because we knew that if we could do something towards the settlement of that strike, you would not chastise us; you would probably praise us. So we immediately sent for the people involved in that dispute, first, in the hope of settlement, and second, because we felt that an actual examination of a concrete case would give us a good idea of the broader picture.
In the first instance we failed. In the second we have, we think, accomplished something, and we believe we learned a great deal about the broader picture of labour relations by the action we took in dealing with those who are at present on strike. Aside from specific recommendations which I intend to go over hurriedly before I shall have finished, what else did the committee accomplish? Surely at least it did this. For the first time, I believe, the people of the Dominion of Canada, the broad number who are neither organized labour nor large employers, have received, as I am sure our committee received, a liberal education in industrial relations, and certainly at the moment know a great deal more than they did before the committee met as to what makes the economy of our country tick, what are the problems facing the different segments of our people, all of whom make up our total economy.
In my judgment at least that was worth while, and that is an accomplishment of this committee. I am not one of the I-told-you-so people, Mr. Speaker, but you may remember that last fall, speaking of the matter of labour in this House of Commons, I made this statement, which I think is still true, that no strike and no lockout can long continue in Canada without a certain amount of public 'support; 'because after all, these two elements, employer and employee, great and powerful as they are, are as nothing compared with the great consuming public in this dominion. They cannot operate this country. Temporary setbacks to the ordinary fellow may come, because he is unorganized. But, in pursuing the even tenor of their way through people like you and me, those of us who are their parliament, the ordinary people will continue to be the backbone of our democracy, the backbone of our economics. That will always, I hope and believe, be so.
Now I may turn to some incidents, some subjects perhaps, which were discussed in the committee itself, and I am going to criticize, I hope justly and, I am sure, with restraint, two things in our industrial relations picture which I think require amending. In doing that, I think it is esential that I mention the evidence given by two or three of the witnesses.
I refer first to Mr. Donald Gordon, chairman of the wartime prices and trade 'board. He appeared before us. I had not the honour of his acquaintance prior to that time, and I believe that was true of many members of the committee. We were all greatly impressed by him. I was particularly impressed by his fearlessness and by his power. I am afraid I was not equally impressed-at times only-by his logic. But I give him this credit: he is a man doing a very unpopular job, he is a man doing a very big job. I do not know, as someone said in the committee, who could have been found to replace him. I am anxious'to pay him all the compliment I can, but at the end of the road I was unconvinced, even when he was supported by the Acting Minister of Finance and by the Minister of Labour, that he had made a case for a ten-cent maximum in the rise in wages in the steel business.
I am not saying that he is wrong. I do not say that for a moment. His opinion is entitled to very great respect, and it seems to me he would be a foolish member of that committee, thirty-five amateurs, who would disregard it. Now we are. being frank about this business and I am sure everybody else will be. Certainly I will be, and I have no hesitation in saying to you, Mr. Speaker, that if Donald Gordon, with all his experience, says, "If I go substantially beyond that, I feel I could not control; it would be dishonest to try", then who am I to say, "You are wrong"? The most I can say is that my judgment, according to the old Scotch verdict, would have been, not proven. On the other hand, and I am frank again, when Donald Gordon says that to me, I, an amateur, am not going to come into the House of Commons and assume the responsibility of saying that he was wrong, because-call it cowardice if you like; call it what you will-if he were right and the collapse did come, I would have difficulty facing you or any other honest people in this country whom I know.
I intend to go a little farther with the tencent theory. It was supported by the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott)

and permit me to say very respectfully of the Acting Minister of Finance that he added nothing at

Industrial Relations

all to the evidence of Mr. Gordon. He merely came there with a statement covering six or seven pages and said that Mr. Gordon was right. That is not said critically. I do not know what else he could do; I do not know what else there was to be said.
I endeavoured-and I tried very hard-to find out from the Acting Minister of Finance whether this ten-cent maximum was a matter of government policy. If it were government policy, the farthest he could go would be to say it was his personal opinion. It strikes me that when a minister of finance, dealing with a matter' of finance, gives it as his opinion, it should be government policy whether it is or is not; because, though we heard the other day that this country was not governed by experts, I still think that responsible ministers of the crown, and I am quite sure I am right, should continue to accept responsibility for the things done by persons in the departments over which they have control.
We had a lot of trouble with that ten-cent proposition. Facing us was the fact that in British Columbia fifteen cents had been granted by the regional war labour board. The chairman of the regional board in that province is Mr. Pearson, the Minister of Labour. We had that fifteen cents rate approved by the Minister of Labour on two occasions in the house, who said that it was sound and sensible, and who strongly advised the men to accept it. That put us amateurs in a rather difficult position in trying to form judgments of our own.
May I say at once that the lumber business may be-may be, remember-somewhat different from the steel business. The steel business operates twelve months of the year. The logging end of the lumber business operates nine or ten months a year in seclusion and in faraway places. But let us not forget that there is no ceiling on logs. There is a ceiling on lumber. Fifty per cent of the lumber is exported to places where the owners or the corporation can get whatever prices they care to ask for it. Losses incurred in domestic sales or wages do not matter so very much if they can get it back from Great Britain- because that is where most of it is going- from the United States, and from other places to which these exports go.
May I continue with this ten-cent offer? On the first day of April the prices board granted an increase of $5 a ton in the price of steel. It was plainly said to us by Mr. Gordon that at that time, the first day of April, having made a complete and thorough examination of the position of the steel companies, that in that $5 a ton there was some-

thing for an increase in wages. Mr. Hilton of the Steel Company of Canada told us that so far as he was concerned there was ten cents an hour in that $5 a ton. I say this critically of the government. It seems to me-in fact I am sure of it, and it was sworn to in the committee and I believe it-that if at that time ten cents had been given to the steel workers we would have no steel strike in Canada to-day and the committee on industrial relations would never have been set up. I do not think there can be any question about that.
This brings me to a major criticism, namely, that there has been no direct contact, no proper liaison between the national war labour board and the wartime prices and trade .board. We realize that to hold down prices we must have a ceiling on them, and as a part of that effort we must stabilize wage positions. I do not think anyone in the committee disputed that. What do we find? We find the wartime prices and trade board operating in an airtight compartment. We find the wages board operating in another airtight compartment and no practical liaison between them. Just now we expect to hold the price ceiling, admitting that wages enter into that ceiling as a part of the cost, without these two elements coming together somewhere, is something that I have been utterly unable to understand. The government must accept responsibility for that.
Perhaps I had better read another quotation from the evidence taken before the committee, and it will be the last extract that I shall read. It is a brief statement by Mr. Gordon on that point, and there are many of them. These answers were given in response to questions asked by myself. I am reading from page 343 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee:
Q. But there is no direct contact between you?
A. That is right.
Then a little further down:
Q. Then who does?
A. Well, each board looks after its own job. The wage control board of the government, as far as industry is concerned, and the national war labour board and the regional war labour board; it is a completely separate field in that respect than the jurisdiction of the prices board.
Then a little farther on:
Q. Yes, but let us take steel. Would the increase given by the prices board, and as you have said, there was machinery whereby these men might go to the labour board and find out what portion of that increase belonged to them. That, in effect, was what you have said?
A. In respect to that, I do not want to split hairs, but I do not want to leave the impression that there was anything in the price increase which was ear-marked in the wage increase. That was entirely in the hands of the management.

Indwtrial Relations
Q. Let us admit that, but what portion of that increase would be determined by the war labour board? You do not fix it?
A. No.
Q. And you leave it to the war labour board to do that?
A. That is right.
Q. There was no liaison between you and the war labour board in this specific case?
A. That is right.
Q. So it could be fairly said, with respect to our machinery in regard to prices and wages, that they are entirely separate and there is no direct contact between them?
A. That is right.
Having read that, may I again say, at the expense of repetition, having regard to these elements which enter into prices, how anyone could ever expect the thing to operate without some meeting place somewhere, .particularly in times of stress such as we are in now, is something which is quite beyond me. Let no one think, sir, that I am indulging in mere condemnation of any board. I realized that the regional board and the war labour board have handled and settled many disputes, and have done so satisfactorily. I realize that the prices board has done splendid work in many instances. But here we have reached a pitch, here we are approaching that place in inflation which Mr. Gordon told us may mean collapse. Under these circumstances, the failure to have contact between these two boards at this time is in my judgment inexcusable.
I want to say a word in defence of the position taken by the labour witnesses on the question of inflation. The evidence they brought was roughly that we, the members of the House of Commons, were mentioned in dispatches and that our $2,000 and ail these things were contributory factors toward inflation. Mr. Conroy did present three sheets of double-spaced typewriting, all containing instances of price increases. On the other hand he gave us instances of increases in wages. I am not covering the whole period. I realize, as it was proven, that generally speaking since 1941 wages as a percentage matter have risen higher than prices. The thing we were up against is that in this very year, in this very spring, the cost of.living index has gone up five points. We have had nothing like it, except after the first great war; five points in a matter of months. That is the situation, we are now facing. What they said was this. How is it there can be all these price increases with no strikes-they were not caused by strikes-yet when labour asks for more than ten cents, anything beyond that is inflation? I am not for a moment saying they proved that Mr. Gordon was wrong, but they did 63260-321J
prove to a humble individual like myself that there are two sides to most arguments, and they did produce quite a number of facts in. support of their position. Nearly everyone on that committee was convinced, as I am convinced, that one of the things we most require to take care of industrial unrest is a country-wide labour code. I am for it; there is no doubt about that. Why, in this particular case we are up against differentials at Dosco which do not exist at other places, and so on. speechtext:
Yes. I was not talking about old age pensions; I should like to, but not at the moment. That course could be very easily followed. The next recommendation was:
That in the interval much closer contact be established between the wartime prices and trade board and the regional and national war labour boards.
I have covered that fully, and I need not repeat my argument. That was a criticism, and nothing would be gained by going into it .again. The next recommendation was:
That matters coming before the regional and national war labour boards be handled expeditiously.
That is in there for this reason. If my memory serves me aright we were unanimous on recommendation No. 1; I may be wrong, but in any event we were nearly unanimous. That paragraph merely means this. The men who appeared before us did complain of delays. Those complaints were answered by the vice-chairman, I think it was, of the national war labour board; but whether or not they were answered the fact remains that the process was somewhat slow. This is not a judgment against anybody; it is a suggestion, and a very wise suggestion, for expedition in dealing with disputes of this kind.
Paragraph 2 of the recommendations is simple; I do not need to argue the point, because it is admitted;
2.	Your committee is convinced that continued price control is only possible with a reasonable measure of wage control.
The next recommendation is;
3.	Your committee recommends that a measure of union security should follow certification.
As far as I am concerned I am prepared to accept holus-bolus the remarks made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) in this house last fall during a discussion of labour matters, in regard to the implementation of this clause. Then I want to spend perhaps a moment or two on the next paragraph:
4.	Law being the basis of our society, your committee condemns:
(a)	the policy adopted by some unions and some employers of disregarding the legal machinery provided for adjusting wages and settling disputes;
(b)	breaches of the law of Canada by the use of physical force or otherwise either by employer or union.
I suppose some bright people will ask, "Why did you include the employer?" Certainly at present all the newspapers are picking on

the worker for being in breach of the law; and he is. There is no doubt about that. As far as I stand and those who stand with me, the right of a man to go to work without being molested while going and coming is his; and let me hope and pray that it always will be. On the other side, however, those of us who have lived for some time know there are what are called goon squads, and these goon squads are not confined to labour. They can be hired in the larger cities of Canada to-day, and within the memory of all they have been so hired. So these words are not put in just to get us by; there is meat in each of them, and something should be done on the other side of that picture because surely we are entitled to live in a country where the enforcement of law is in the hands of officers duly appointed to enforce the law be it on one side of this picture or on the other side. If you will look again at the Toronto Star of to-day's date, a little lower down on the right-hand side of the page we see a heading over an interview with Mr. Millard in which he urges the prosecution of the Steel company for triple pay. If a company are in breach of the law in respect to triple pay they should be prosecuted the same as anybody else. But at the end of that article he makes the charge that there were gunmen in that plant who wounded five of these workers; and if that is a fact prosecutions should be launched in that connection. So I think we are all in agreement in this house. We will never permit the law to be used as a strike breaker, I trust, but we will permit it to be used and will insist that it be used so that individual liberty shall remain and a man may go where he will.
Now I turn to the next recommendation, which was put in at the request of the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll):
5.	Your committee recommends that the law of picketing be studied with a view to its modernization and clarification and for the purpose of making it more effective for the protection of the rights of all elements in the community.
I have promised to assist the hon. member any way I can in respect to that, but I do not think we need weary the house with it just now. Then I come to recommendation No. 6. We had a great deal of trouble with this one, particularly with the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), who led the attack, in which he was joined by the hon. member for Spadina and one other hon. member whose name I have forgotten for the moment. What we were seeking there was this, and it comes as perhaps the joint thought of all. Perhaps I hadi better read it:
Your committee recommends that the Minister of Labour may. at the request of either party to an industrial dispute, and if he deems fit,

Industrial Relations
either before or after a strike is in progress, direct that a strike vote be taken under government supervision to determine the wishes of the men affected as to whether a strike will take place or otherwise.
What does that mean? It means this: It is -the right of the secret ballot. To copy the words of the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), it is the introduction of the rule of law into these matters. I am not criticizing the upper bunch in the top drawer of union leadership. But I am supporting, and will continue to support, and I trust this house will continue to support and affirm the principle of the secret ballot in any organization of this kind, just as we have it when we are elected to come here to the House of Commons.
It has been suggested that the words "before or after a strike is in progress" are meaningless. Well, let us look into the coal mining business, because I know at least a little about it. There we have what are known as pithead strikes. They are illegal. It simply comes up when someone has been called a son-of-a-gun by a foreman, or something of that kind. Out they go from the washhouse and they say, "Nobody goes down the mine to-day, daddy. We are on strike." In other words, the strike is on before anyone has voted or has a chance to vote.
So what we are saying, in No. 6, is that in strikes of that kind, after the strike is in effect the minister can go in and take a vote of those persons concerned. That is all it means. In my judgment-and I know I will be criticized for saying it-section 6 will be the biggest advance-when it is made into legislation-in labour legislation ever made at one time by this House of Commons. I have no doubt about that. I am told that it will create resentment throughout labour across the country. Well, if it does, I cannot help it. If assuring to the individual, by ballot, the right to determine his own future is a matter of resentment by labour, against me, then let them resent it. I am for the man who wishes to run his own life in his own way. .
I now turn to two simple ideas of my own.
I have said before, publicly, and I have said it privately, that any man in the Dominion of Canada who is willing to work is entitled to a wage, not just a living wage, but a wage which will keep him and his family in some comfort and with some of the luxuries of life. That is where we stand; that is where we should stand; that is the foundation from which all these wage rates are negotiated.
May I add this-and with this the house will be pleased to know that I shall close- that I think one of our main troubles in industrial relations in Canada lies in the fact that management and labour do not know one another. It seems to me a strange commentary that I am permitted in this House of Commons to rise in my place and say that Mr. Millard and Mr. Hilton, the director of the union and the manager of the company respectively, had to be introduced to one another in this building by Mr. Brockington.
Mr. Speaker, we shall never have decent industrial relations, peaceful industrial relations, until we are ready to credit the other chap with some honesty and some intelligence.
I realize that in some places you cannot do that. I realize that we had before us one witness who, in my judgment, did not seek a settlement of the strike, but who sought only continued commotion. But that is not true of the great majority. If we can but get to know one another, and have employers and the representatives of employees really get to know one another, and to learn that the qualities of each are not bad, we shall have made some advancement. The office calls the organizer a communist; then the labour organizer in turn calls the office a fascist, and that is about the way things begin in labour relations in Canada.
So that in this, as in all other things, with a bit of tolerance, a bit of understanding, with a broader outlook aside from our own business, and with an understanding of what we are doing for the future of our whole economy, no one need worry, nor need anyone despair for the future of this great Dominion of Canada.
