speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I have some right and some qualifications to speak on this question. It is a great pleasure to me to follow a former hero of old Wesley college, and an opponent in athletic contests. He gave a good account of himself then, and he has given a good account of himself to-day.	.
W'hen I sat across the way I stood up and commended the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) upon his appointing a real labour man to the position of Minister of Labour. I said this, Mr. Speaker, that the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) had a record second to none in Canada as a labour leader, a labour organizer and a man who had backbone enough to stand up and hit out from the shoulder. I do not think there is any man in Canada who has taken more punishment than our Minister of Labour. But when I used to take part in the manly art I found it was the man who could take the most punishment who often won out, because he could bide his time, take it in his stride, and then hit when he had the most chance for success.
Industrial Relations

If there is a man in Canada who should have the gratitude of the workers of this country, it is the Minister of Labour. I am tempted to quote from Bums these lines:
Man's inhumanity to man
Makes countless thousands mourn.
He has taken it in his stride, and has stood for peace, order and good government. I commend him for it, and will support him to the limit. Any angel Gabriel who came down *here to-day to take the position of Minister of Labour would have one of four or five organizations, or perhaps all four or five of them, on his back. If that Minister of Labour did not support the C.I.O., then he would not be good enough for them. If he did not support the C.C.L., he would not be good enough for them. If he happened to support the Catholic Union in Quebec, there would be those who would say he was out to hold Quebec for the Liberal party in Canada.
Our Minister of Labour has a job; it is a man's job, a job for a man with a head on his shoulders, a man with red blood in his veins, with lots of health and strength who would not run away from a job like this. That is our Minister of Labour.
It has been stated by many experts that we have the best labour code produced by any country in the world, and for that the minister must be commended. I do not ask the house to take that on my word. When the labour code was passed this appeared in the Montreal Herald:
Mr. A. :E. Mosher, president of the Canadian Congress of Labour, in a press statement made on F ebruary 17, 1944, and which is reported in the Montreal Herald, under date of February 18, 1944, is quoted as follows:
"In my opinion the regulations governing the wartime labour relations, as adopted by the federal government, will go a long way toward meeting the demands of organized labour for a satisfactory labour code ana I feel the government deserves credit for its action.
One of the privileges labour unions appreciate most highly, and for the maintenance of which the free peoples of the world are fighting, is the right to criticize a government when its policies or actions are considered objectionable: but it would be unfair if it failed to be equally outspoken in commending any government for what appears to be a sincere effort to promote good relations between workers and employers.
In view of the difficulties which were inevitable in handling the unprecedented problems involved in legislation of this character, it is scarcely to be expected that there will be entire satisfaction at the outset, but I believe the government has done a good job in the circumstances and I do not hesitate to congratulate most heartily both the government and its officers who were responsible for drafting the regulations."
I could refer to what was said by Mr. Harold Crabtree, chairman of the executive of the Canadian chamber of commerce, when [Mr. Mclvor.l
he paid a tribute to the minister and to the government. The official publication of the trades and labour congress, namely, the Trades and Labour Congress Journal for March, 1944, contained the following statement on its editorial page in connection with the appointment of a labour relations board:
We have at all times protested and resisted the introduction of orders in council which, in our opinion, were unnecessarily drastic. We will just as readily commend our governments when legislation is enacted which, in our considered opinion, is in the best interests of the many thousands whom we represent, and we state without fear of successful contradiction that order in council P.C. 1003 is a good piece of legislation and warrants expressing our appreciation to the government for its enactment.
The labour congress of Canada expressed its appreciation, and other leading organizations in Canada have paid a tribute which practically amounts to saying, "Thanks to you, Mr. Minister of Labour." I know the Minister of Labour has had his testing times and I confess that I was guilty of putting him through one. When the seamen were on strike I called him at one o'clock on a Sunday morning. I received a call from the trades and labour council of Fort William that eighty-four men were stranded there who had to be at work on Monday or they would suffer a $20 a day fine. Sometimes it is not easy to get a man on Sunday morning because he may be at church or he may be some place else. I took the risk of calling the minister and I told him what had happened. He replied-, "Dan, we will do our best for these men." As I say, eighty-four of them were stranded at the head of the lakes because those who wanted to break the seamen's strike had taken away their boats. As a result of the minister's action, these men received their fares and were able to go back to work. So again on behalf of the seamen's union of Canada, I say, "Thanks to the Minister of Labour."
I was surprised and pleased at the discussions that took place in the industrial relations committee. I was surprised to see two leading members of the C.C.F., both keen and honest men ready to do the right thing for Canada, taking sides and voting against each other. It shows that there is some hope even for the C.C.F. notwithstanding what some people may think or say.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
I stand for a square deal for the man who toils. He should have a living wage. The thing that causes a great deal of

Industrial Relations
trouble in Canada and in other countries is the fact that a man has to toil six, eight, ten or more hours a day and is unable to get more than a living wage. Then he sees the man who employs him able to go to California in the winter time, able to send his children to the university. If the mother of the children of that worker puts up fifty cents an hour for a music lesson for a child, they have to skimp on something else. Somebody has said that he would rather see the great masses of the citizens of our country living in peace, in health, with sufficient food and clothing and opportunities to educate their children, than a few rolling in wealth. I do not think anybody wants the irritable discontent that follows when our workers are not properly looked after.
I stand for a living wage for every toiler. If he does not get it, it is just too bad. I must admit that the fault is not always on the one side. There are those in this house who will remember the Winnipeg strike of 1919.
I took part in that strike. I interviewed the striking committee, although I was not one of those in that position. When the strike first started we were sure that the strikers were bound to win. Then the strike committee called out the bread wagons, the milk wagons; they shut off the water in some places, and they called out the firemen. I told the strike committee then, "You have gone too far." Public opinion just came back with a surge and beat the workers. It took them years to get back again what they had lost. It was not until the Liberal party in this house gave labour a square deal that they regained their ground. They have had better success than they ever had in the history of Canada.
The secretary of the trades and labour council of Fort William says that there has never been better legislation than that which was passed by the Mackenzie King government, using my own words. I would pay a tribute to the trades and labour council of Fort William because I do not think there is anything better in Canada. We have been remarkably free from strife. The head of that union was able to find time to lead a campaign to provide $40,000 for a Salvation Army hostel. That shows that he has a heart for the man who is down and I want to pay him a tribute.
As I said, strikes are not always caused by one side. The hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) has suggested that there should be a secret ballot, and I think the same way. I support the resolutions which were passed by our committee. I think they will go a long wav to help, and I think we should have a secret ballot. I can tell the story of one man, an employer of labour, who said, "If any man
comes to this ballot box to vote in favour of a union in our place he will be kicked to some place out of here." Of the two men who were the first to vote, one had had twenty years service in that plant, and they both lost their jobs. I heard of rival unions that took a strike vote in a plant. They had two boxes with a union man standing at each box, one for "no" and one for "yes". That is not secret enough. A man should have a secret vote; and I think this resolution will be helpful.
In this committee I heard a statement from one of the members about which I have thought a good deal. He said that there were three stages in the development of a union leader. One was the agitation stage. I think we had an example of it in our committee, and I did not agree with that particular individual. Then there is the administrative stage, when he is willing to go a little farther and listen to what the other fellow has to say. Then there is the cooperative stage; and in that class I would put men like the late Tom Moore, who was, willing to go all the way and lead his workers in cooperation with capital. Capital and labour must get together. You may have a cure for this trouble; I have it. Labour and capital must get together;^ if they do not, both will lose out and something else will take their place.
I have here a quotation from the Ottawa Journal:
Perhaps both management and labour in this country still have to learn . . . that there exists a public interest which is over all. The mood of "the public be damned," whether coming from capital or labour, has no place m our modern life, and the sooner capital and labour come to know that and to act accordingly the better it will be for them and for us all. Labour will have to learn that there can be no hope for it, no gain for it ever, beyond processing ot our resources, which is our only wealth, at reasonable profit. Capital will have to learn that labour is more than a commodity, more than part of its raw materials, that it is entitled to share justly in the fruits of production.
I cannot close better than by giving a summary of a resolution passed by a group of men in Fort William, headed by a gold medallist, Doctor R. K. Dewar. These gold medallists have a little more grey matter than most of us, and if it runs in the right channel it can do some good. The resolution they sent to me stated that the men who put their money into a business have a right to a fair profit; the management and the labour who put their lives into it have an equal right, not a commodity right, but a living right to a living wage; and if there is anything available over and above that, it must be divided between those who toil and those who put their money into the business. I am glad to know that at the head of the lakes we have business
Industrial Relations

concerns which are sharing their profits with their workers; and, so far from being dead, or nearly so, they are the most vigorous businesses at the head of the lakes. When a man gets a living wage he has more incentive to produce, and the more that is sold, the better it is for him and for those who employ him. The more production there is, the more money is available for the employer and the better the income for the individual.
In closing, I would just say that to my mind the remedy for our trouble to-day is to observe the old injunction, "Love your neighbour as yourself". If you hate your neighbour there is little hope for you; if you follow the leadership of Him -who said "Love thy neighbour as thyself", you will go far on the way to personal and industrial peace and good will.

As one of those who had the honour to serve on the industrial relations committee I wish, in saying a few words, to associate myself with what the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) said in regard to the chairman of that committee. It has been my experience also that the chairmen of our standing and special committees of parliament are always fair and conduct the proceedings with dignity. I may go farther, and associate myself with the hon. member for Calgary West when he said: that it was a pleasure for him, to work with all the members of that committee-up to a certain point.
I am sorijy, however, that I cannot go so far with him as to approve the recommendations made by the committee. Not that, with one exception, there is anything wrong with those recommendations, but in my opinion the report is an anti-climax, following the urgency of the circumstances under which the committee was set up, and that urgency has not lessened during the time the committee was sitting; if anything, it has become more grave.
Let me quote briefly from the speech made by the hon. member for Calgary West the day the committee was set up. When he proposed the committee he said this as reported in Hansard, at page 3489:
My suggestion is this, that this house should immediately set up its industrial relations committee. To that committee should be invited__
yea. brought if necessary-those persons who might not like to come. I think I am not saying anything very unusual, because there, and only there, can meet the big three, so-called-the three important people, the consumer, labour and management in industry.
A little later on, he said:
Then it seems to me to these people on strike, and those who are talking strike, such as the meat people the railway people and so on, this parliament should say: We have given you the last and best tribunal this Dominion of Canada TMr. Mclvor.]
knows. Come there with your problem. Meet your opponents face to face in the presence of that great referee, the consumer of Canada . . .
The consumer of Canada, if that is what the committee is, having met these people face to face, having heard their troubles, comes to this house with a solution. What is it? To call a dominion-provincial conference to set up a labour code; make a recommendation condemning the use of force in the settlement of disputes; urge that a committee be appointed to investigate the law on picketing; recommend that a measure of union security should follow certification; assert that price control is only possible with a reasonable measure of wage control.
All of that, of course, I can support. But there is nothing in it that can do anything toward settling these disputes which are disrupting the economic life of the country at this time. They do not touch the fundamental causes of these disputes. The one I do not agree with-and I might as well deal first
with the recommendations of the committee_____
is No. 6. The hon. member for Calgary West read it; now let me read it:
Your committee recommends that the Minister of Labour may. at the request of either party to an industrial dispute, and if he deems fit, either before or after a strike is in progress, direct that a strike vote be taken under government supervision to determine the wishes of the men affected as to whether a strike will take place or otherwise.
I imagine that the words "or otherwise" means, or continue". The hon. member for Calgary West mentioned the sort of circumstances in -which a vote of this nature would likely take' place. He said it might happen in a mine where the men might come to the pithead- some morning and, if the superintendent or the foreman did not take off his bat to the men as they came to work, they might say, "We will go on strike". Those were not his words, but it might be anything. But that is not what is in this recommendation.
It says something quite different and does not refer to a pithead strike or to any particular kind of strike. It refers to any strike, befbre it begins or after it begins; and if this is approved- by this house, the Minister of Labour, having the approval of this house, can take a strike vote in any industry where there is a strike. He can go over the head's of the elected representatives of the workers' organization and take a vote to determine, without reference to the organization at all, whether the men want to go back to work or stay on strike.
If there is a better way of destroying the trade union movement, that way has not yet

Industrial Relations
been called to my attention. I say that as definitely as I can because it is implicit in this recommendation:
. . . either before or after a strike is in progress, direct that a strike vote be taken under government supervision to determine the wishes of the men affected as to whether a strike will take place or otherwise. .
That is, or continue. Before dealing wiith that, the hon. member for Calgary West referred to the interview of F. B. Kilbourn, the controller appointed in the steel dispute. Mr. Kilbourn says this-and let us see in what respect it differs from the recommendation made by the committee.
However, if it is put up to him-[DOT]
That is, the settlement of the strike.
-he said he believed his first step would be to find out the facts of the situation. He said he thought this could only be done by a thorough examination into the desires of the workers. He said he believed this could be done only by having all workers in the affected plants answer a set of questions. The survey, he said, would be conducted as balloting in an election is conducted, in complete privacy. The worker would go into a booth and write his answers and the sheet, which would bear no method of identifying the worker, would be deposited in a ballot box.
He does not advocate that .the government should take the vote, or that it should be taken under the supervision of the Department of Labour, but taken by some impartial individuals. But he did not say who is to choose the impartial individuals? As a matter of fact, Controller Kilbourn is proposing, in this interview, the recommendation made by the committee in No. 6 of the report. If iwe do not like it we had better be quite sure of that before we adopt these recommendations.
As far as the report is concerned, I think I can leave it at that. The other six or seven recommendations are not of great value; they are neither here nor there. If they have no great value, at least they are not harmful. But as regards No. 6, as I warned the committee, so I warn this house. If you pass this you are putting your stamp of approval exactly on what the hon. member for Calgary West denounced when it was proposed by Mr. Kilbourn.

It is not deep at all. A part of the preamble to the report states:
An opportunity was thus afforded for the first time for labour and management to present to a committee of parliament such statements as the terms of your order of reference required and such are on record.
It may or may not be strange, but although numerous labour organizations made representations to the committee to be heard- more labour organizations than in fact were heard-no employer, as far as I know, had asked to come before the committee. We had three employers of labour before the committee. They were all asked to appear, and no other employer of labour in Canada expressed any desire or even gave any hint that as far as he was concerned there was a committee of parliament investigating the cause of industrial unrest in Canada. If I may be allowed the expression, Canadian employers treated the committee with the utmost contempt. Perhaps that in itself should give the key to the cause of labour unrest in Canada, namely, that employers want to ignore labour in the same manner as they ignored the parliamentary committee. As far as they are concerned, the industries of Canada should be run for the profit of employers and not for the benefit of the Canadian people.
I do not think any member of the committee will deny or can deny that the real cause of the labour disputes that are at present wrecking the economy of Canada is the demand by the workers for increased wages. That is one side of it. The other side is the insistence of the government that wage increases of over ten cents an hour will not be allowed. That was the question we always came up against in the committee. As a matter of fact other questions really were not of great importance.
As was pointed out by the hon. member for Calgary W'est, the Minister of Labour had intensified the situation by putting his stamp of approval on increases of fifteen cents an hour in one section of Canada and then stating that in other parts of Canada increases of over ten cents an hour would not be allowed.

Of course I mean it; there is no reason why I should not.
There are a number of factors which enter into our industrial difficulties. The first is the natural hostility-I say "natural hostility"- which exists between workers and employers.

Industrial Relations
It is the hostility which exists between buyers and sellers, no matter where you find them. In this country the employers have not yet reached the stage where they are willing to accept their employees as citizens of the community and deal with them as citizens with equal rights with themselves.
One of the things which impressed me in the various documents placed before the committee is that, despite all the education, all the laws and regulations which w-ere passed during the war years, the employers of Canada are still opposed to meeting and negotiating in good faith with their employees. When you have employers acting in that way you will have employees who will use their power to the limit, the moment they feel that they have power. Let me quote briefly from some of the documents which were placed before us. I have in my hand a report on Brunner Mond, by Magistrate J. A. Hanrahan, who was appointed a commissioner in this dispute by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell). The report states:
The contract between this company and workers expired last November. Amendments suggested by employees were submitted last September. Members of negotiating committee complain very bitterly of what they describe as the disheartening delaying tactics of company from then until July of this year-
That is from September of last year until July of this year. Do you wonder there are strikes?
-which prevented a new agreement being completed and finally made strike action imperative. This is a factor that has undoubtedly-contributed to the present very firm demand for some form of union security and warrants the conclusion that it comes ' from deeply affronted employees rather than having been inspired by union officials.
Then from the same document:
The general good will and earnest desire of this local to act fairly with company is further evidenced by fact that when strike was called no objection was taken to main office staff, engineers of pump house and purification plant, boiler room and engine room, engine crew to haul coal, crane operators to load cars of coal and remove ashes, the chief engineer, the fire protection chief and the chief electrician for safety remaining on duty. As you are aware this is somewhat contrary to local practice. The company does object to what they describe as illegal picketing.
I have wired appeals to Mr. Robert W. Atkinson, sales manager of Brunner Mond of Canada, Montreal, and Mr. Carlton Bates, director of operations, Solvay process, Syracuse, N.Y., whom workers believe are really determining company policy in this matter for a modification of their instructions to Mr. J. B. Aylesworth, K.C.
But no matter what the appeals were, these people do not want to deal with their employees, and they are willing to disrupt the 63260-322J
industry of Canada in order to defeat the efforts of their employees to organize. I was also interested in the report of Judge Cameron, who was commissioner in another dispute. I thought his report, in putting blame on both parties, was most fair and in that way was in direct contrast to the report on the steel strike, made by Commissioner Roach. In his report, at page 985 of the reports and proceedings of the industrial relations committee, Judge Cameron said:
The extreme rigidity with which the strategy committee regarded the "seven point programme" is seen in the case of one company which had negotiated a contract in February, 1946, and which resulted in substantial wage increases. The union stated that in spite of wage increases then given and after discussion of the "seven point programme," it still insisted that an additional 20 cents an hour should be granted by that company.
Then he continues:
On the other hand. I think it fair to say some of the companies have not approached the negotiations in a realistic manner. The union's programme was presented to the companies as a basis for local negotiations more than six months ago-
Those who recall that there is a rubber strike in progress in Canada at the present time, which has been going on for some two months, will remember that the rubber workers had tried to negotiate for six months before the strike was called.
-and in a number of cases concrete counterproposals were never made by management. I am satisfied that a more reasoned approach to the problems involved, rather than a mere rejection in toto of all the requests made, would at that stage have brought about satisfactory results on a plant basis in some cases.
The reply of the committee to that is a recommendation that the government take a strike vote, after the employees have been on strike for two months or more, to see how they feel about going back.
A good deal has been said in the press and elsewhere about the attitude of trade union officials. A remarkable report or finding was made by a justice of the Supreme Court of Canada, Mr. Justice Rand, last fall in the Windsor automobile dispute. I do not know how many hon. members have read it, but if they have not already read it I suggest that they do so. They will find that this justice of the Supreme Court of Canada does not agree that the labour leaders or trade union leaders in Canada are irresponsible. He says:
I have had an opportunity of sizing up the leadership of this union so far as it is represented by the committee of negotiation. The members are all of English-speaking origin and British citizenship. They have impressed me as being made of the stuff of which ordinary Canadians are made. With the exception of Messrs. Burt and MaeLean who are on leave of absence
Industrial Relations

from General Motors at Oshawa as international representatives of the union, they are men with seniority in the Ford plant ranging from ten to eighteen years. They conducted themselves in negotiation with intelligence and reasonableness. I have no doubt their dominating interest is the job of those they represent in that industry and that their object is to attain for those employees and their families a secure and self-respecting living, which seems to be the object of most Canadians. That aim is legitimate. whether or not attainment is possible.
It has been suggested that the union officers, as other labour leaders, are primarily concerned with the maintenance of their positions and power and no doubt some of them have experienced stirrings cf that nature. But union organization is admittedly necessary in the present set-up of our society and we cannot expect these men who have gifts of leadership-and it is by such leaders that movements against wrongs are initiated-to be quite free of those human frailties from which only a few saints escape. The only effective remedy for abuse of this nature is a greater democratization of the union.
And may I say that greater democratization of the union cannot be brought about by taking away the powers and prerogatives of union members by insisting that the government may take a strike vote at any time it wishes. We cannot get democratic unions unless we give union responsibilities, and insist, too, that they discharge those responsibilities as citizens.
The second reason-and I have dealt with it before-for industrial disputes is the refusal of employers to deal fairly with their employees. The third, in my opinion, is the failure of the government to impress upon employers, upon workers, and upon the public generally, the urgent need for production.
Even before the war came to an end, a cry went up for the removal of all controls- "Let us get back to business as it was". Of course that meant business as it was before the war when employers had hundreds of thousands of unemployed who could fill any jobs which might be offering. Hon. members fell for that sort of thing. Demands were made on the government every day from this side of the house by the official opposition for removal of controls. I was amazed to see how quickly those lion, members were impressed by Donald Gordon when he appeared before the committee.
Consequently there is no recommendation from the committee stating that in its opinion it would be better to grant the increases in industries where they are asked, and get those industries operating. With our improved productive capacity, in my opinion we would in no time catch up with demand. We would not be looking for commodities to meet needs, but for needs which could take the commodities we had to offer.
[Mr. MncInnis.J
I do not think we have any idea of how the productive capacity of this country has increased during the war. Even in Great Britain, where the whole economy of the country was put to war uses, they have made a remarkable, one might almost say a miraculous come-back in the production of ordinary consumer goods. But in Great Britain employers, labour, the government and consumers got together to discuss production, and the needs of production.
I have here an item from the London Daily Herald of July 31, 1946, which states:
Important plans for close consultation at top level on economic matters between industry and the government were outlined in parliament yesterday by Mr. Ness Edwards, parliamentary secretary to the ministry of labour.
This consultation is to be through the minister of labour's national joint advisory council, on which the trades union congress and the British employers' confederation are represented.
That council, superseded during the war by a smaller body, is being reconstituted, and will hold its first meeting soon.
Mr. Edwards said:	"there is no intenton of
departing from the government's declared policy of entrusting responsibility for determination of terms and conditions of employment to the joint machinery of negotiation between employers' and workpeoples' organizations.
"But the government considers that it will assist and reinforce this machinery of joint negotiation if there is the closest possible contact between the two sides and the government."
I notice, Mr. Speaker, that you are going to tell me my time is up. I shall just say that on various occasions I have urged the Minister of Labour to bring the different factors in industry together and to impress upon them the urgent necessity for production, not only for our own welfare in Canada, but for those things for which our young men died during the war. That is of the utmost importance. But it cannot be accomplished with Pollyanna proposals such as are contained in the report of the committee on industrial relations.
Mr. DAVID A. CROLL (Spadina): Mr. Speaker, I wish to join with the hon. members for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) and Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) in paying tribute to the chairman of the committee.. Perhaps I could sum up in these words, he was a happy choice.
I enjoyed working in the committee with all its members at all times. I was particularly impressed to-day when the hon. member for Calgary West drew on his wide knowledge and experience, his broad understanding, and gave us a treat in what I believe was a brilliant summation of what took place in the forty-nine sittings of the committee. But it left very little for me to say. To follow the hon.

Industrial Relations
member for Vancouver East, with his thoroughness and knowledge of his subject, leaves even less.
I do believe this, though, that it can fairly be said the country expected too much and got too little from the committee. Rather than devote myself to a discussion of the various portions of the report, I shall discuss only one or two phases of it. The hon. member for Calgary West has already indicated that I opposed section 6. Members of the committee know that full well. 1 consider it important, however, that this section be understood by the house; we have already had some misunderstandings.
I feel strongly in the matter, and this prompts me to read the section once again, because each one who has read-it has emphasized a different part. It states:
Your committee recommends that the Minister of Labour may, at tire request of either party to an industrial dispute, and if he deems fit, either before or after a strike is in progress, direct that a strike vote be taken under government supervision to determine the wishes of the men affected as to whether a strike will take place or otherwise.
What does that mean, as a practical solution of labour disputes which have already been carried to the point of strikes? I suggest that we should examine the clause carefully. Let us assume for the moment that a strike is in progress. Hon. members know full well that this means that all or part of the men have walked out. It means, too, that a picket line has been established. It may be that the machinery in the plant is silent, or that machines are being manned by employees who are not on strike. It may also mean that machines are being manned by others who have been brought in as strike-breakers.
The recommendation says that the minister is empowered to order a vote at the request of either party to a dispute. Once a strike has taken place, all the minister can determine is something that is self-evident. A vote by whom? It says, "The men affected." We have the right to assume that "the men affected" means both sexes of all ages. I believe that was the intention of the committee.
Let us see who are the men affected by a strike vote. No one will deny that the strikers, the people who are on the picket line, have a right to vote. No one will deny that those who disagreed and continued production, whether they passed through the picket line or whether they were parties to a lock-in, are entitled to vote. The third group would be the persons who were hired by the company since the strike began and who are dependent upon the company for their present and future livelihood, the people who are
commonly known as strike-breakers. The fourth group included in the term "the men affected" would be the office help, the messenger boys, the stenographers, the foremen, the superintendents, the technical people right up to the vice-presidents.
Can anyone suggest that they are not all men who are affected by the strike? Can we afford to accept this recommendation and turn our backs on the Rand formula which brought about a new equation in labour relations, which said in effect that union security equals company security? In my opinion that was the most progressive and socially minded document on labour relations that this country has enjoyed in the forty years since the industrial disputes act was passed. We ought to give it an opportunity to see if it will work before we disregard it.
The decision was first given in the Ford case at Windsor. I have known of the labour relations in that company for twenty years. The annual report of the Ford Motor Company of Canada Limited was presented before the committee, and a portion of it indicated that they were in complete and absolute agreement with the Rand formula. More than that, it had brought peace to the plant; it had brought unity to the plant; it had improved the man to man relationships. It has been said that the Ford Motor Company was decentralizing, and one of the reasons offered was its labour relations. However, to-day plants on the outside are being sold and they are moving in again to Windsor. They are doing this because labour relations are such that they once again feel they can carry on in Windsor.
The Rand formula laid down fundamental principles for this country. Mr. Justice Rand made the bold statement that all workers in a plant benefit from union representation; that all should contribute but that they need not join the union unless they so wished. He declared that in case of a strike every employee, whether he be a union member or a contributor, should have the right to vote. No one could quarrel with that and I think this house generally endorses it. In effect he said that those who share the benefits should also share the penalties. If we accept the committee's recommendation we turn our backs on Mr. Justice Rand's decision and the government will be disowning the very child that it brought into being.
The other part of the clause speaks of a vote under government supervision at the request of either party to the dispute. If we have a strike, we have already had a vote and the union has had a mandate. Will the union ask for another vote? Can anyone conceive of any possible circumstance under which the
Industrial Relations

union would ask for a vote? Let us examine the other side for a minute. I think we can appreciate that there will be occasions in a dispute when an employer would consider it advantageous, particularly if all the men affected would have the right to vote. Let the strikers' morale sink to a low point. Let the compaign reduce the resistance of the strikers' families. Let the plant be loaded with strikebreakers. Let the employees who have not gone on strike be paid triple pay. Let those things happen, and the employer will certainly call for a vote.
Let us assume for a' moment that the employer has picked the time properly. A vote is taken and the minister then determines that a strike does not exist. What happens when the minister says that there is no strike? It is obvious that it then becomes a disturbance of the peace. It is inevitable, if we are to have law and order in this country, that either the police or troops will have to be called in to deal with the matter of the disturbance of the peace. The only alternative is that production resumes on the employer's terms. That is what I think this clause means and I so submit to the house. I think the government is put in an impossible position, because under these circumstances it may well be accused, not without some justice and some truth, that it is in the business of strikebreaking.

Before this house rose at six o'clock, I was dealing with section 6, and pointing out to the house that this section lends itself to many and varied interpretations. My second point is that section 6 in its present form will defeat collective bargaining, which is now the law of the land under P.C. 1003, in that it will result in a greater reliance upon the state, which betrays a lack of faith in collective bargaining and the democratic processes of unions. If section 6 stays "as is", it will inject the government into almost every labour dispute, with the result that in the final analysis it will be fixing not only wages but working conditions, and it may well be interpreted to be attempting a legislative short-cut to bring about industrial peace. That, I submit to the house, has already been tried. May I point out that the German labour front-and I apologize to the minister for even mentioning that as a labour movement in the same breath with our own-was TMr. Croll.]
modeled exactly on that principle. In times of a dispute they immediately used a referendum, with the result that unions lost their independence, lost their identity, very shortly became instruments of the state, and faded and vanished from the scene completely. I think hon. members will agree with me that it would be a catastrophe to weaken responsible trade unions, because they have a niche in our way of life and they belong.
My third point is based on the words "before a strike is in progress". I assume that would mean the negotiating stage. Let us assume that the company offers six cents and the union counters with twelve cents. The minister is then put in the difficult position of having to decide if six cents is a fair offer, and he may step in and take the vote. I submit to the house, is it not quite possible that without a dislocation of industry the final result would be that the union would receive nine cents? Those who were members of the committee will remember this particular evidence. Stelco first offered five and a half cents, then ten cents, and finally eleven cents-ten cents straight and a cent for holidays.

holidays there, which made up another cent. Mr. Brockington's report indicates it. Algoma made an offer of six cents and finally raised it to eight cents. I do not think Dosco ever made an offer; it was consistent throughout. But I remember very well Mr. Justice Roach giving evidence and using words to this effect: "When they close the books you will have had the final offer." It is a matter of judgment whether you have had it or not. He was then talking about a conference which he was holding in Algoma on July 8. As a matter of fact the evidence discloses that at that very time when Mr. Justice Roach thought he had the final offer, an offer of ten cents was being made here in Ottawa. That is not a criticism of Mr. Justice Roach; he had every reason to believe what he did, but it is difficult to say when you have had the final offer.
I think the minister can perform a useful function without departing from his nonpartisan role. What we want is a vote of the men who are concerned, a secret vote by qualified voters. We are opposed to telegraphed votes and we are opposed to voting deadheads. With that I think the house and country will generally agree. And, rather than the clause as it stands, it occurs to me

Industrial Relations
that a clause reading something like this would be more useful: "That a strike vote will be taken under government auspices of members of the bargaining agency and other employees within the bargaining unit who contribute to the maintenance of the bargaining agency." There is a natural desire on the part of the non-union employees, the management, the public and the government to find out how great the sentiment is in favour of the strike. Is the strike desired by the members of the bargaining agency, or is it a mockery for the furtherance of minorities' ambitions? There can be no objection to that, and I certainly have none. My objection is that the present clause is so ambiguous that it becomes highly dangerous, and under it unions will be compelled to fight what may appear to them and may actually be unfair or unjust decisions; they will be forced to fight for their very existence, and they will often be placed in the invidious position of striking against the government, with the result that it may lead to such industrial strife that only two sections in this country will profit, t'he people on the extreme left and the people on the extreme right.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
In the steel strike and the other strikes in progress or threatened in Canada we are witnessing a clash between the old order and the new, between the old order of scarcity, of want, and of fear, and the new order of plenty and of freedom from want and fear. On the one side we have the government and the companies striving to force this nation back into the shackles of scarcity; on the other side we have the workers' unions struggling to strike from labour's limbs the age-long fetters of poverty. More specifically, it is a conflict between the labour unions and the government of Canada. In a deeper sense the battle is between the workers on one side and the orthodox financial system on the other, between progress and reaction.
The task assigned your committee was, and I quote from the terms of reference:
to investigate, immediately, all issues connected with and appertaining to the present industrial unrest in Canada.
And again:
and to report their findings and conclusions to the house.
Before proceeding, I should like to join the other members who have spoken in a word of appreciation of the members of the committee. I found the chairman fair and conscientious; I found the steering committee industrious and thorough; I found the members of the committee devoted to their duty and, in very large measure, tolerant and patient. I enjoyed every minute of the long periods we spent together.

Industrial Relations
The report of the committee aims to be unbiased, not to take sides. It aims to be judicious, not to aggravate the difficulties, and it aims to be helpful. But. the report falls far short of expectations-the expectations of labour, of industry, of the government and of the country. What the committee did was to hear briefs for labour, for industry, and for the government against granting labour's request, and for the government to show why its machinery for dealing with industrial disputes is adequate.
Without desiring to reflect at all on the steering committee, I may say that, as I review the whole situation, it does look to be a peculiar bill of fare for a committee charged with the responsibility with which this committee was charged.
The committee found an apparently impossible situation. I believe every member of the committee was consciously or unconsciously aware of that fact. We had labour demanding in effect fifteen cents an hour increase and a 40-hour week. We had industry affirming that it cannot or will not pay that amount. We had the government insisting that any wage increase above ten cents will cause inflation. We had this fact; that the 15-cent increase to the steel industry would be taken as a pattern all over the country and would cause demands in every industry for similar increases. We found each increase in wages tending to cause a corresponding increase in the cost of goods and consequently in the cost of living; and each increase in costs of goods tending to force demands for higher wages. This was a situation which I think everybody realized and it caused everybody a measure of frustration. There was this additional truth underlying the whole situation, that if costs of production in Canada were increased too far through wage advances, then two serious results would come about. In the first place, Canadian industries would be unable to sell their goods in Canada in competition with goods of a similar nature coming in from outside, and, in the second place, Canadian industries would be unable to sell their goods in competition with the goods of other countries on the world's markets.
It would be extremely difficult to find more complications for one committee of men to deal with in one month. What could possibly be done to provide a square deal for all? The whole Canadian economy was thus in reality found to be in an economic strait-jacket. No matter how much we produced, men could get no more. As a matter of fact, the more we increased our production in Canada, the more we increased our real wealth,

in all probability the worse would be our poverty. Obviously, something was radically wrong. The committee was not given an opportunity to investigate that which, was wrong or what might be done to correct the strange paradoxes which were discovered to exist, the strange conflicts and contradictions.
The committee failed to do a number of important, things. It failed to get. evidence to support Donald Gordon's contention that an advance of more than ten cents would cause inflation or an increase in the cost of living. I was astounded at the readiness, almost the abject humility with which the committee listened to this man lay down the law to them, accepting him without question. After seeing these same men act in the House of Commons, I found myself at a loss to understand what had happened.
The committee failed to get a clear picture of the situation as regards inflation. Donald Gordon said that an increase of more than ten cents would cause inflation, but we never had clearly defined for us what inflation was. It was never laid down in so many words, and we never demanded that it should be so laid down, that, after all, inflation is only a rise in prices. It was never laid down to us that the ordinary cause of inflation is a shortage of goods. It was implied several times, but never specifically stated. The committee never had given it the causes of inflation. There are three of them; first, the scarcity of goods in relation to the amount of money in circulation in the. hands of the consumer and coming into the markets to buy; second, an increase in costs which will force up the price, and third the manipulation or the writing-up of the price. These causes of inflation ware never laid down definitely before the committee.
The committee never learned, or never had the evidence brought before it, to show the safeguards which might be used against inflation or the remedies for inflation. It was never shown, in any scientific sense, to what extent the causes of inflation are operating in Canada to-day, the extent to which the safeguards against inflation are being employed in Canada, or the extent to which the remedies for inflation are being recognized and used by the Canadian government, or are available to the Canadian government, or could be. made available to the government, or could be used by the government. The result was that the whole concept of inflation was left nebulous.
The committee failed to get evidence to show whether each of the steel companies could, without increasing prices of its products, pay the minimum wage demands of the union.

Industrial Relations
We had the statements of the companies, but never an examination in any scientific and thorough way by anybody, by men appointed by the government to do just that thing and give a report to the committee. We never learned exactly what is the financial position of each of the companies, how fat it is, to use a common and rather vulgar expression, how much of the fat the Canadian people have the right to oblige the companies to lose. The committee never had set out before it how much capital is legitimately invested in each company, or how much was put into it; how much of its savings had been reinvested in equipment, how much watered stock is in the capital of each company. I was astonished to find that matters of that sort were never outlined to us in any detail.
We never had brought before us how much yearly profit each company had made, or the average yearly profit over say twenty-five years, which I think is an important matter, or whether or not that rate of profit was reasonable; that is, whether it was enough in comparison w'ith what ought to be reasonable. We never had a standard set before the committee to show what should be the reasonable profit of a company. We never had the question answered, is that profit rate large enough to encourage men of means to invest their money in this industry, or is that profit rate large enough to stimulate the company to optimum production, or is the financial strength of the company all that is required to enable it to compete successfully in the Canadian market against steel coming in from other countries; and then to compete in foreign markets? Until these questions could be answered regarding each company, it was obviously utterly impossible for the members of the committee to form any accurate conception whatsoever as to whether the companies could pay.
The committee failed to get evidence to show whether, under the present financial system, it would be economically feasible for the government to subsidize each of the steel companies sufficiently to enable it to pay increased wage demands without increasing the prices of the product, to subsidize either with money from taxation or with money borrowed. This matter was never canvassed, yet is one which I think was an important issue pertaining to the problem which the committee had to study.
The committee failed to get evidence to show whether or not the wage demands of the steel union are excessive. At present prices in Canada what is the wage required to support a family in health and decency? No evidence whatsoever was submitted. Apparently the government gave no attention to that problem, whereas it would seem.to me that that matter should have been gone into with great care as applied to Hamilton, Sault Ste. Marie and Sydney.
The committee never did get evidence to show whether, under the present financial system, the Canadian economy can stand to nay the union wage demands, financially or physically. Considering the fact that there would be corresponding increases throughout all industry, when we remember the broad terms of the problem submitted to the committee it must be surprising that no such evidence was brought before the committee which was supposed' to examine into all the issues pertaining to the industrial unrest in Canada.
The committee never did get evidence to show whether or not, under the present financial system, it would be practicable to bring down by subsidies the cost of living to the level, say of January 1, 1945. This matter would have had an important bearing upon the wage demands of the union. We never went into that question.
The committee never got evidence to- show whether or not each of these steel companies, namely, Steleo, Algoma and1 Doseo, is essential to the welfare of the Canadian people. It did not get evidence to show whether, and to what extent, the manufacturing of steel for export is essential to the Canadian economy. It failed to get evidence to show whether or not government ownership of these three steel companies and of other companies if necessary would enable the Canadian government to provide the workers with a living standard of decency and health without increasing prices, without impairing production, without jeopardizing the economic and competitive stability of the companies, without curtailing freedom to strike and bargain collectively.
The committee did not get evidence to show whether and to what extent debt-free money created by the state could be safely employed to pay either subsidies requisite for bringing down the cost of living, or wage bonuses to the workers, thereby increasing their incomes without increasing the cost of producing steel. Certainly this would be an important issue pertaining to the whole problem of industrial unrest in Canada. Lacking information as regards each of these important issues which I have mentioned, connected with and as pertaining to the steel strike as a manifestation of the present industrial unrest in Canada the committee, I submit, failed to report conclusions upon the matters of wage rates and hours of labour, the

industrial Relations
two vital bones of contention in the whole struggle. This fact I think must be looked upon as being surprising.
When the committee commenced its operations I believe everybody realized that the two vital questions being asked were whether we could grant wage increases in the amount demanded and whether we could give the workers hours of labour which they requested. Tet we made no report bearing on either one of these essential matters, largely because we failed to get the evidence which would have enabled us to form a sound opinion upon these two most important matters.
We found, Mr. Speaker, that the problem was exceedingly grave, as I have already indicated.

speechtext:
That is good: I hope it will not become necessary again. It is an easy matter just to start talking, you know, and make it absolutely impossible for an hon. member to be heard even by those who wish to hear him.
The gravity of the problem, Mr. Speaker, becomes manifest when you consider the psychology which is abroad in the country at the present time. There is a dangerous psychology on all sides. First, with respect to labour, the present labour leaders in Canada have seen strange things in this glorious country of ours. Let us not forget for a moment that these memories have been in their minds all through this struggle. After the first world war, in the twenties, the labouring people saw a period of almost unprecedented prosperity in Canada. Trade was buoyant; production was bountiful; credit was relatively easy to

get. But the incomes of the great rank and file of the Canadian people were meagre; they were shamefully low.
Then suddenly in. 1928 and 1929 something happened. Then came the baffling thirties. All the farms, the forests, the mines, the fisheries and the factories were still in Canada. All the splendid people of Canada were still in this country; skilful, ambitious, industrious, patriotic, patient and cooperative; the same people who eagerly produced and gloriously fought in world war I; the same people who within ten years were to dazzle the world with their magnificent production for world war II and their splendid and heroic striking impact wherever they found1 the foe.
All through the terrible thirties, I say, these great resources were in Canada; the same Canadian people were present in Canada; the warehouses were bulging; Canadian store shelves were sagging with goods. Yet Canadian industries stood half idle; Canadian workers, yearning for work, languished in idleness or rode the rods or camped on the roadside, while a Liberal member of parliament honoured the men who were to become the heroes of Dieppe, of Sicily, of Ortona, of the Falaise Gap by styling them "spineless yaps and street-corner bums."
Canadian misery was widespread. "There is no money" was the plea in parliament and press, on platforms and in the offices of bank managers. The cry was repeated and reiterated dismally, " There is no money."
Then suddenly war broke out. Money soon was everywhere. It sprang up like grass blades in the spring. Whereas previously we had spoken of a .million dollars with considerable respect, if not reverence, we now began talking and thinking glibly of billions; billions for tanks, aeroplanes, ships; billions for guns and gasoline; billions for pork and eggs; billions to lend abroad or give away. Government officials and cabinet ministers declared sternly that what was physically possible would be made financially possible. The only factors limiting our war effort were to be materials and man-power.
By 1944, though more than one million of our finest producers were overseas fighting, Canada was able to produce an almost stupendous quantity of tanks, aeroplanes, guns, ships and so on; of food, clothing and other necessities with which to supply our fighting and auxiliary forces; food and supplies to provide for our allies; food and clothing for ourselves, to provide the people at home with a higher standard of living than they ever enjoyed before in history.
Now labour and all thoughtful citizens in Canada want to know; is our Canadian peace

Industrial Relations
effort to be as successful as was our war effort? Is our peace effort, as was our war effort, to be conducted upon the principle that what is physically possible will be made financially possible? And if not, why not?
This question is in the minds of the labouring men all over this country, and the whole situation causes a dangerous psychological setup. Already labour has been told that the Canadian Liberal government cannot afford money for the payment of subsidies to keep down the price of milk for the poor man's family, to keep down the prices of jams, jellies, corn syrup, corn starch, raisins, prunes and other vital commodities for his table; to keep down the price of clothes for himself or his children.

If anyone supposes that this sort of thinking is not in the mind of practically every labouring man in Canada, then he needs to learn what is in the minds of the labouring men; he needs to get ::hem talking. We experienced poverty in the midst of plenty in the hungry thirties. Are we being led toward an even more hopeless poverty in even more hungry fifties? And shall we, as Canadians, tamely submit to this sort of thing?
With respect to the psychology in industry; the industries of this country themselves, the very industries which are now struggling against labour, saw depression. They saw overproduction; they saw lack of markets; they saw their factories partly idle; they saw increased overhead, and by reason of that fact they sustained losses. Now they see the repetition of that depression coming, in which there will be shortage of purchasing power and failure of markets both at home and abroad. They see productive capacity greatly increased; then they see taxation very burdensome already, and their troubles increasing.

Yes; you are deeply interested in solving the problems of the nation; wonderfully interested!
Now, as to the people of Canada as a whole, from coast to coast; they also fear the future. They fear unemployment; they fear depression; they fear an increased cost of living; they fear ruinous taxation which they are now enduring and by which they are being crushed. They fear painful shortages. This is the psychology obtaining throughout Canada; this is the background against which this strike struggle is being carried on.
There simply must be a solution which will be a real solution, not a return to former ways of doing things. Public feeling is running high. There may be grave disorders. There is economic necessity for a solution different from anything we have had before. I am going to quote a passage from the report of the Bank of Canada for 1944, by Graham Towers. This passage indicates quite clearly that the writer saw there would have to be great changes, but we see no evidence of any contemplation of such great changes by the present government. This is one of the things which distress and dishearten the people as a whole. I quote from page 12:
It seems likely, however, that at least 4,700,000 workers will be available for employment in civilian jobs, or at least 1,500,000 more than the number employed in that sector of the economy at the present time. A working force of this size, at present rates of efficiency, will be able to produce a vastly greater volume of civilian goods and services than Canada has ever known before.
Is it to be supposed, I interpolate, that industry does not realize that?
By the same token, a vastly increased volume of consumption and capital development will be necessary if this output is going to be fully absorbed and high employment maintained. The adjustments required will clearly be of unprecedented magnitude, and bold planning on the part of labour, farm and business organizations, as well as governments, is urgently needed.
There is a warning of extremely great portent, That was in 1944, but there appears no inclination, and there appeared to be no inclination before the committee to take into consideration matters of that kind.
May I turn to another set of figures at page 9 of Graham Towers' Bank of Canada Report of 1946. A set of figures is given there which indicates the tremendous productive power of Canada. In 1944 she produced $11-8 billion worth of goods and services, and in 1945 $11-4 billion worth. All such amounts of goods and services must be purchased in the post-war years somehow or another. The government spent in 1944 $5-4 billion on those goods and
Industrial Relations

services, and shipped them away to be wasted. And in 1945 the government spent $4-5 billion.
This vast expenditure will fall off, now that the war is over. What is going to take the place of that purchasing power in the Canadian economy to absorb Canadian goods? Any thoughtful person will ask that question with great apprehension. The people of .Canada, because of the war incomes they were enjoying in 1944 spent $6-2 billion, and in 1945 they spent $6-5 billion, whereas in 1938 the poor, unfortunate Canadian people were able to spend only 83-7 billion. We are rapidly returning to the 1938 position, as the economic incidence of war is falling off.
Now the question arises: What is going to happen with all this tremendous production? One of the men representing industry definitely referred to that three or four times in his evidence-the anxiety he felt regarding the future.
It is a well known fact that the Canadian income in 1941 was exceedingly low. I have already put on record twice this year evidence to sho.w that in the year preceding June 2, 1941, for all Canada 32-9 per cent of Canadian wage-earners were receiving S450 a year or less; 28-7 per cent received between 8450 and 8949 yearly, and 91-5 per cent of the total Canadian population received less than $1,950 a year.
It must be obvious to anyone that some tremendous measure must be taken, to replace the purchasing power which evidently is going to fall off. What is being done? This whole matter was actually part of the problem!. It should have had scrutinizing attention from the committee.
May I offer what would have been the Social Credit proposals, if the Social Credit group had been making recommendations to parliament. We would have recommended, first, that Mr. Millard's wage offer to Mr. Brockington was fair and reasonable. I believe practically everyone agrees with that.
We would have recommended, second, that the government should reopen the plants at once oni the basis of Mr. Millard's offer.
In reopening the plants the government should adopt those requisite measures which might appear best calculated (1) to avoid further price increases in Canada and1 (2) to avoid impairment of the economic stability of the steel companies.
We would have recommended, third, that the government should immediately begin to take all necessary steps to reduce the Canadian cost of living with the objective of bringing that cost of living back to .the level prevailing

on January 1, 1945. That objective should be attained not later than January 1, 1947, and, if possible, by November 1, 1946.
Fourth, the money necessary to implement these recommendations, the government should obtain by a series of "win the peace" victory loans, the first of the "win the peace" victory loans to be offered in the fall of 1946.
Fifth, the government should appoint a royal commission on industrial relations to examine into each of the issues the committee failed to investigate.
The royal commission should study with care the many issues the committee ought to have studied in order to be able to make an intelligent report on the whole of industrial unrest throughout Canada.
The reasons for the recommendations I have mentioned are these:
First, Mr. Millard's wage offer to Mr. Brockington was not excessive. Canadian industry can produce enough goods to provide a standard of living for Canadians consistent with such an income as this wage rate would allow. This wage will do very little more than give health and decency to workers. Workers ought to be able to save. Canadian producers need more purchasing power in the hands of consumers to supply the producers of Canada with home markets.
The government should reopen the plants on the basis of Mr. Millard's offer to Mr. Brockington, because production in Canada has already been far too much impaired1. The loss we have already sustained in the Canadian economy is almost irreparable. Confidence among both employers and employees in Canada ought to be restored at the earliest possible moment, and the government ought to lead the way into the new order of abundance..
All during the war we heard talk about the new order that was to be. Even on one occasion the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) waxed' enthusiastic and talked about a new heaven and a new earth. Why in the world does he not come to grips with our economic problems, and lead the way into that new order? Why do his ministers stand as blocks in the way, while labour has to struggle and risk its all in order to force the government into something like a progressive policy? That is a question any ordinary man would ask. The government ought to lead the way.
In reopening the plants it should adopt measures which will avoid price increases. The wage increases could be given as a government bonus, which would' not enhance costs of production. Failing that, the government could subsidize plants to enable them to absorb costs of wage increases.

That is right; I am not singling out any man. It is easy enough to laugh at someone who is outlining something which people do not understand. But let me tell you, that they will laugh on the ether sides of their faces if we do not get this problem solved in due time. There will be no laughing matter about that.
Measures resembling the two I mentioned before interruption, financed ultimately with state-created, debt-free money would enable, industry to pay living wages, without adding to the costs to the consumer.
Provided that Canadian production were first stimulated to a point at which needs of Canadians were supplied, the increased amount of money resulting from these measures would not cause inflation through scarcity of goods and services. This is the only genuine, legitimate cause of inflation. All the talk about funny money and rubber money, and all that other contemptible nonsense we hear in the house and in the country has no foundation at all either in logic or in reason. Let men take the pains to get the economic facts into their minds, and form their policies on the basis of those facts. The government could bring down the cost of living to the January 1, 1945, level by subsidizing the prices -of certain key products. The withdrawal of government subsidies on certain commodities caused or permitted the rise in prices that resulted in mounting living costs in Canada. The opposite process obviously would reduce living costs. Therefore, to speak of bringing back by subsidies, the cost of living to the standard of January 1, 1945, is not fantastic.
Money for the present should be raised by "win the peace" victory loans because production in Canada is at a low level. Consequently state-created debt-free money could not be used at the present time without inflation because there is a shortage of goods. Canadian supply is too low to meet the needs of Canadians. There appears to be already in the hands of the consumers more money than there are goods and services to buy with that money. This means that there would be an inflationary tendency owing to scarcity of goods.
Scarcity of goods must be overcome. Production must become buoyant, abundant and universal in all our industries. The time will then come when there will be more goods in the markets than there will be money in consumers' hands to buy. Then the state will be able safely to create debt-free money to represent the surplus production. Such debt-free money, will then be available to the government to pay subsidies and bonuses to maintain stable and equitable prices and to maintain stable and equitable wages. But industries must go into action immediately. Social Crediters would advocate debt-free money under normal circumstances in Canada but we suggest that debt money be used now, because of shortage of goods and because the people of Canada generally do not understand enough about money to welcome debt-free money. We must tide over the present crisis.
A royal commission ought to be appointed to learn for Canada all the essential facts about our economic and financial system and learn
Industrial Relations

what possible measures can be taken to reform our economic and financial system so that we may be able to go into a new order of abundance. Let a royal commission discover for us the means of ushering in and establishing a new order of plenty for our Canada, a land of plenty in this age of plenty.
Social Crediters earnestly suggest that a way out of our industrial unrest can be found; it has been found. Social Crediters are confident that there is a way by which we can bring into being a new order of abundance and freedom, freedom from want, fear and curtailment of our personal liberties. Social Crediters urge in all sincerity that the road to the new order of abundance and freedom can be found through the applications of the principles and the technique of Social Credit. Let Social Credit point the way.
I say to members of the house who have desired to question me that this matter will come up again when we are discussing the estimates of the Department of Labour if all goes well. I can and will then answer all questions which hon. members may wish to ask pertaining to the principles, the technique and the philosophy of Social Credit and point out how those principles may be applied to the problem which confronts us.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
It was, indeed, a sad day for Canada when that union was in force, much too sad to be passed over now as "unutterable nonsense."
On February 9, 1945, there appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail the following:
Buck explains why minister beaten
Tim Buck, national leader of the Labour-Progressive party, issued a statement yesterday-attributing defence minister MeNaughton's defeat in the Grey North federal by-election Monday to "reactionary Toryism, helped by the suicidal policy of the C.C.F."
Mr. Buck's statement said:
"Only cooperation between the forces of labour and the progressive Liberals can stop the Tory offensive, and appealed to all progressive people and especially honest supporters of the C.C.F. to condemn the policies which are bringing Canada to the brink of disaster."
On March 9. 1945, there appeared in the Toronto Telegram an editorial which I quote in part, as follows:
L.P. Party's Election Manager Becomes a Canadian at Last.
Word comes from Ottawa that departmental action has been taken to relieve the Labour-Progressive party of the embarrassment of having as its national election manager a man who is not a Canadian.
