speechtext:
If the hon. member for Mackenzie had not been interrupting so much he would have heard it.
How far will this Liberal tentacle reach out to satisfy its demand for complete control?
This government has had no definite labour policy. If the present laws are not satisfactory, then they should be rescinded. If they are satisfactory, they should be enforced. It would seem that no one in the government has courage enough, or if they have the courage, they are not allowed to say what they really think, or to state a definite policy and stick to it.
The people want leadership, sane, sensible leadership, but it is not forthcoming from the government. So they accept the leadership of radicals and communists who make all kinds of ridiculous promises to the workers but have no responsibility. No doctor can cure a condition by simply treating symptoms. He must find the cause. Likewise, no government can cure the present economic conditions by merely salving over wounds. Too much thought is given to votes-more salve for the open wound, where actually some surgery is required to close the wound.
In recent years labour has accomplished much in the way of improved wages and working conditions, which I believe just and right. But let us compare this with the position of agriculture. Taking 1913 as the base period, when industrial labour and agriculture were equal at 100, the position of labour as of 1945 was approximately 264 while agriculture stood at approximately 162, or a difference of 102 points. I quote from the Searle index:

Industrial Relations
A bushel of Canadian wheat to-day, according to the records of the Searle Index has a purchasing power over the things that farmers have to buy for their living and production of only eight per cent more than it had in 1913, whereas the hourly wages of Canadian industrial labour have a purchasing power to-day of 64 per cent more than these same wages had in 1913. Why then, we ask, should not our farmers enjoy the fruits of this increase in the Canadian standard of living that has been brought about by Canada's natural economic progress since 1913, and which increased standard of living is enjoyed by Canadian industrial labour and by many other groups of individuals? In considering all these prices, it is to be remembered that the Canadian dollar of to-day has only the same purchasing power over the things that farmers have to buy as 62 cents had in 1913.	*
This condition cannot go on. There must be some reasonable equalization, or agriculture will fail to produce and money will mean very little if the necessities of life are not available in sufficient quantities to supply the needs of the people.
Thousands of farmers left their farms to work in industry during the war. They found it easier, fewer working hours, less responsibility, workmen's compensation, unemployment insurance and city conveniences in their homes. But they must eat, and with this added burden of production on fewer farms, and with the cost of production rising steadily, agriculture finds it more difficult to carry on.
I think I can safely say that as far as agriculture is concerned the present demand by labour for a 40-hour week is the breaking point. I am not saying that labour is not entitled to a 40-hour week, but I do say that agriculture cannot compete in the labour market at that figure. It would either require the farmer or his family to do more of the work or put on two shifts, which would increase considerably his cost of production. With price control in effect, agriculture must come to this government for an increase in the price of farm products. This in turn increases the cost of living and labour demands higher wages. In order to meet these demands, industry feels it should have more for its product, and round and round we go; where we stop nobody knows.
I see logic in labour asking a one-cent increase in wages per hour for every one point of rise in the cost of living index, but Mr. Millard, in answer to a question in the committee, did not seem willing to allow wages to go down in the same proportion if the cost of living index went down. He likened it to an insurance policy, but there was no mention of premium payment. If price control is to be continued until we get past the point of dangerous inflation, then everyone must be prepared to sacrifice a little for the sake of
Canada and our future. We must plan ahead, not stumble blindly along thinking only of the present.
While I recognize the right of every worker to join the organization of his choice, I also believe in the right of every worker to abstain from joining any organization or to retire if he is a member and if that be his wish. I cannot agree to the view that the right of any individual to earn a living must be dependent upon the payment of dues to any organization. A trade union should see that its leadership and union activities are such that every worker wants to belong. Collective bargaining will never fulfil the hopes held out for it, nor will there be stability in labour relations unless increased right afforded labour is accompanied by the assumption of increased responsibilities, and unless there exists mutual confidence between the parties that an agreement once entered into will be honoured.
Strike action to date has lost for Canada millions of dollars' worth of export contracts. It is clearly the responsibility of the government to settle it. This can be done if our national leaders have the will and the courage to face the problem fairly and fearlessly.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply):
speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate by reason of my own special interest in restoring industrial peace to Canada. I had taken on the obligation as Minister of Reconstruction which seemed onerous at the start but which became impossible during the last six weeks when labour unrest came to the boiling point.
Let me say that the committee that has been studjdng the labour situation has been, in my opinion, well worth while. I am not going to give a review of the work of the committee. That was done in a manner both brilliant and accurate by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith). I want to say I think the members of the committee have a better understanding of the calibre of labour leadership in Canada through hearing the labour leaders that appeared before them, and perhaps a better understanding of the calibre of industrial leadership from the few representatives of industry whom they heard.
I believe there is one thing that struck every member of the committee, and that is that of the labour difficulties which were reviewed by them, all had failed to follow established procedure of government for the settlement of disputes, and everyone of them had to be rated as an illegal strike. Another thing which I think must have impressed itself on the committee was the obstacles put in the path of any possible settlement of the steel strike. That was not an ordinary dispute
Industrial Relations

between, employer and employees. It was converted into a dispute among several employees, all with different types of production and different financial problems, andi groups of workers in several industries, many of which were quite dissimilar from other groups involved in the dispute. The demand was that all be settled by a common formula.
It was quite impossible for any of the principals in the dispute to settle with their workers by bilateral bargaining. That was obvious. For example, if Steleo had wished to settle its dispute with its employees it was quite unable to do so unless by some means clearly beyond its powTer it was able to induce Dosco- to settle on another formula with its employees and to induce Algoma ,to do the same. It was obviously a dispute directed toward- the government, for only by the exercise of arbitrary powers by the government could the many factors in the dispute be resolved. The dispute was not even confined to basic steel. The problems of basic steel have some resemblance as between one plant and another, though even in basic steel the products turned out by Algoma are not the products turned out by S-telco, and the products turned out by both are not wholly the products turned out by Dosco. But it went far beyond that, because the settlement of the dispute depended not only on the settlement of these three disputes, but the terms of settlement were required to apply for all the subsidiaries of all three companies.
Arguments were -used about the hardships of the work in front of a blast furnace, but I personally was unable to follow the logic which said that because the worker at the blast furnace is entitled to high -pay, the operator of the tack machine in a subsidiary plant is entitled to the same pay. I simply mention that to show the complications facing anyone who undertook to find a solution of the steel strike in any single plant based on the demands of the bargaining agency of the workers. However, we heard evidence from the labour leaders involved not only in the steel strike but also in the rubber strike, the automobile strike, the chemical strike and the strike in the electrical industries. We all got a view of the leaders; we heard the presentation of their cases. I think we all formed an opinion as to whether labour in Canada is being wisely led in one industry as against another, and we got a fair idea of the problems of management in dealing with its workers under present-day conditions.
In the steel strike we -were faced with a situation which was unique. The wartime prices and trade board had recognized that

it was unable to hold the line which had been established in February of 1944 and which had been maintained up to May or June of this year. The pressures had become too great; too many forces over which the wartime prices and trade board had no control were operating to bring further pressure on the price ceiling. Canada is a heavy importer of goods, particularly from the United States. In the United States a substantial increase in prices had occurred which was reflecting itself on manufacturing costs in Canada. _ It has usually been the practice of the wartime prices and trade board to deal with price increases based on proven costs; in other words; the costs must be established first, presented to the wartime prices and trade board, and price adjustments, if considered necessary by the board, are made in the light of proven cost figures. However, when the steel adjustment came along-and the price of steel had not been materially changed except in a few items since 1939-it was realized that an adjustment of wages was imminent. The wartime prices and trade board could not ignore the wage increases in the United States; nor could it ignore the fact that substantial adjustments were being made in other industries in Canada and would be demanded in the case of steel. Therefore, in making an adjustment of steel prices they made an allowance for wage increases.
The committee heard Mr. Donald Gordon on price stabilization and the effect of wage increases on that problem. I think every member of the committee was- profoundly impressed by Mr. Gordon's evidence. However, it did emerge that the price allowances which were made when steel prices were adjusted amounted to about ten cents an hour on labour costs, as nearly as the board could determine. I wish to say again that that determination could not be accurate because the costs vary in the case of different steel producers. However, I think members of the committee came to the opinion that a wage increase of ten cents was about all the increase in steel prices permitted. Was that a reasonable increase? The view has been taken that it amounted to nothing much at all. After all, a ten-cent increase in steel across the board is fairly substantial in percentages, particularly as it applies to the lower paid workers. I presume that over the average it- amounted to somewhere between twelve and fifteen per cent across the board, and in the case of low paid workers it amounted to considerably more than that. It was considered reasonable, through the fact that a good many settlements had been made or were being made currently on that basis. Great industries such as the pulp and paper

Industrial Relations
industry of eastern. Canada, the forest industries of eastern Canada and the great nickel industry had been settled on the basis of ten cents an hour across the iboard. Therefore management, in presenting its claim to the wartime prices and trade board and the wartime prices and trade board in assessing that claim, could reasonably forecast an increase of ten cents an hour for labour in basic steel.
A good deal of pressure was brought on Mr. Gordon by members of the committee to fix that allowance exactly. Under pressure, Mr. Gordon admitted that ten cents an hour was about the figure that the wartime prices and trade board had in mind. But he also tried to convey the opinion that price and wage stabilization is not an exact science.
Canada has been more successful than any other country in holding down its cost of living and in stabilizing its wages; but it differs from certain other countries in that it has not proceeded by exact formula. In the United States the Little Steel formula was regarded as the formula by which permissible wage increases could be determined. It was a complicated formula. One factor was the date and the amount of the last increase in pay; the cost of living was an element in the formula, and there were certain other elements. However, we all recall that while the Little Steel formula remained the standard for some months, it had to give way under pressures which even that exact formula could not stand.
From the commencement, Canada did not attempt to place wage control under price control. It set up two stabilization boards, one for prices and the other for wages. The intention was that the board in charge of the regulation of wages would make such adjustments in wages as were indicated. The board could not start from a standard base, because everyone did not enjoy the same wage or even the same relative wage in one industry as in another. But that wage board was authorized to make wage adjustments. The wartime prices and trade board had a somewhat secondary position, because it was its duty to make price adjustments which would take account of costs arising out of wage adjustments. The relationship was not as close as certain hon. members of the committee thought should have been the case, but all I can say is that throughout the war period this dual system of control seemed to work and each in its own sphere did a job in stabilizing the commodity under its charge.
Under pressure, Mr. Gordon stated that ten cents was the limit he believed the price index could absorb and still be kept under control.
I suppose, if Mr. Gordon had been subjected to close cross-examination he would not have
been able to prove that this figure should not have been nine cents or eight cents or possibly eleven cents. However, he was giving his expert opinion as to what he considered to be the breaking point in setting the level of a general wage increase across Canada. I know of no better expert opinion. After all, Mr. Gordon has been in charge of price control since its inception. He had a magnificent record of service before coming to that position, and I think every Canadian citizen will say he has carried on magnificently since taking over that task. It is all very well to say he did not prove his point. I do not think he attempted to prove his point. I think he attempted to give the committee his best judgment, based upon his experience and upon the facts before him, which certainly were more complete than the facts before anyone else on that committee. In any event, the committee in its wisdom decided that it could not overrule Mr. Gordon's judgment.
The committee was not directly charged with the duty of settling the steel strike. However, it felt that this strike was the basic labour problem of the moment, and undertook to do what could be done in that direction. Therefore the committee chose a conciliator of its own to supersede the former government conciliator, and asked Mr. Brockington to bring the parties to the dispute together and attempt to arrive at a solution. I think the committee felt that Mr. Brockington did all that could be done in attempting to reach a compromise settlement. His difficulty was that, before he entered upon his task, management had stated to the committee its maximum offer and labour had stated to the committee its minimum terms, and there was a wide discrepancy between the two. However, Mr. Brockington worked with management and with labour for several days and worked out a compromise settlement which I think members of the committee felt could have been accepted by either side. However, while he drew slight concessions from management and slight concessions from labour, the gap was too wide to bridge and Mr. Brockington had to report that he could usefully offer no further services in settling the dispute.
It has been said during this debate that the dispute could have been settled for five cents. That is, ten cents was ordered by the controller ; it was already in effect, and it has been said here that an additional five cents paid at some time in the future would have settled the dispute. Well, I suggest that if hon. members will read Mr. Millard's offer they will find many other conditions involved besides the five cents, which would have been an obstacle to any settlement. For example, there
Industrial Relations

were three "musts". First was the removal of the Sydney five-eent differential. The question of the removal of that five-cent differential has been before the regional board and the national labour board and has been refused by both. To make that a "must" in settling any dispute with the Steel Company of Canada is, of course, to put an insuperable obstacle in the way of any settlement.

Exactly; nevertheless it has been made a "must". The hon. gentleman -proves my point, as I am sure he intended to do. Then the general wage increase was to be made retroactive. That was agreed to without difficulty; that is obviously fair, and management accepted it as such. Then there was the adjustment of 5i cents. That was a "must"; and the only condition that could be arbitrated was the time at which that adjustment would be applied during the current calendar year. Several items were referred to arbitration. I simply mention the extraneous matters that were brought into a dispute, which would have been difficult enough had each company been bargaining with the union separately on behalf of its own employees, and which became practically impossible of solution when no management was free to bargain with its own employees without also bringing about bargains between other managements over which it had no control and other employees over which it also had no control.
I believe the committee brought forth recommendations that will be helpful in future in dealing with labour matters. I believe we were all surprised at the unanimity which prevailed during the in camera sessions of the committee. I will say that during the course of the proceedings of the committee I do not think any member made any move designed to improve his political position. In listening to this debate, I consider it regrettable that many hon. members should talk politics rather than talk a settlement of labour disputes. I hope we can bring the debate back to the high plane of the discussions in committee, as we proceed with this matter. As I say, we attained a high degree of unanimity except with respect to recommendation No. 6. It did not seem to me there was a great area for disagreement

in regard to that recommendation. Its purpose was to prevent sporadic strikes, strikes not brought about through the use of normal union machinery, but brought about by small groups acting without notice to the vast body of the workers.

speechtext:
No, but I think my hon.
friend will agree that was stated to be the purpose. As to the methods of arriving at the purpose, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) had one method and other members of the committee had another. The other method happened to be chosen. The provision is simpiy this, that if a strike is threatened, or if there is a sudden outbreak of a strike, either side in the dispute may apply to the Minister of Labour for a vote, imder government auspices. The Minister of Labour is not bound to take that vote, the proviso being that at his discretion he may order a vote under government auspices.
It has been said, as it was said in committee-and quite properly-that if the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) were always to be Minister of Labour, that would not be a dangerous weapon. But let me suggest this, that the Department of Labour in this country is staffed by experienced labour men. I believe any Minister of Labour would ask the advice of his experienced advisers as to whether in a particular dispute they considered it advisable that a government-supervised vote be taken. Should the Minister of Labour decide that the majority of the employees were being dragooned into a strike through illegal action on the part of certain of their leaders, or a certain group in the industry, there is the possibility of the Department of Labour's stepping in and deciding the question as to whether or not a vote should be held, under democratic methods, and either authorizing such strike as legal, or denoimcing it as an illegal strike.
I believe that is a constructive paragraph in the report, and is a paragraph which will not be abused. I must say I find myself unable to follow the argument which says that it is destructive to properly conducted and properly organized labour unions.
Meantime, while the committee was sitting, strikes in a number of basic industries were in progress. Not only have they paralyzed industries directly affected, but they are extendihg to industries not directly associated with any labour dispute. That situation is most acute at this moment. There is scarcely a section of the country which is not beginning to be affected by these strikes.

It seems to me that a situation can get so bad that it becomes impossible, and I believe this situation has reached that point. I believe there must be an early solution-

Mr. Speaker, as one of the members of the committee I want at the outset to say that I consider the committee to have been of great value to parliament and to the country. Some hon. members, particularly the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Mac-Innis), have criticized its results, and have stated that the committee's report is an anticlimax. I say to him that in my opinion it is anything but that. There are many forwardlooking recommendations made in the report of the committee. Although I join with him in regretting that the committee was not able to settle the steel strike-even though it was never charged with the duty of settling that strike-I do not think he can say that the concrete fact that no settlement was achieved amounts to an anti-climax. After all, we were not the body responsible for the settlement of the steel strike: the responsibility for that is and always was that of the government.	For the committee to have
attempted to suggest in detail what the terms of settlement should be, or to have dictated a settlement, to my mind would have been setting up a 35-headed Minister of Labour- and such a thing would be a monstrosity.

First, there was a proven lack of forward policy to handle labour-management relations and to improve them in the period after the war. Second, there was a great lack of resolu^ tion and, in one case I am going to mention, not very adept handling of crises when they came as a result of that lack of forward policy. Third, there was, of course, the inexcusable action of condoning and therefore encouraging the breaches of law that we have come to know so well this year. I should like quickly to run through those specific criticisms that I have made of the government.
As to the lack of forward policy, our report itself is a gentle chiding of the government for not having introduced of their own volition a year ago, some of the very things we are recommending to meet changing needs now that peace has returned and the patriotic impulse is no longer so strongly there to keep down friction. Without reading the recommendations, I say that those things would have helped us. I want to go farther than that. I want to say that wage control, necessary in war and necessary in the transitional period if you are to have price control, is nevertheless a negation of free collective bargaining. Labour looks upon free collective bargaining, I think, as being next in importance to its right to strike. Therefore, when you impose wage control, certainly you must be careful that in some way you make up to labour for depriving it of its full right to free collective bargaining.

speechtext: I am not sticking up any straw men; far from it, I assure the minister. I believe that if we had free collective bargaining, then many of the wage increases which are asked for now would obviously be possible. The management concerned, not being held under a price ceiling, would be able to grant a little more of wage increases and raise prices rather than have a strike.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext: I want my hon. friend to finish his statement; does he believe in the principle of price control?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
I am going to be longer than I thought I would be. I will say to the minister that I am not as ardent a supporter of price control as he is. I think it is obviously wrong in principle. But I would not have taken off price control on V-J day, and under

the policy which the government has followed until now I would not be able to take it off to-day if I sat in the seats of the mighty. Let us assume that price control is necessary for the purposes of this argument. Then you must have wage control. But if price control were not necessary, then we would have free collective bargaining. If the government is to maintain wage control, as they must with price control they should realize that such a course would cause irritation to labour. However, the evidence clearly showed that they allowed one of the great congresses of labour to lose all faith in the national war labour board and its members.
The government have failed to coordinate their price and wage control policies in a way that, to me, is incredible. They failed to produce a policy that was always a little ahead of the needs of the moment. Their policy was always six months behind. Thus we have had price control being gradually relaxed over a period of a year since the conclusion of hostilities, and we have had three relaxations of the wage control order. One came in January; one came in April, and the third came in June. The relaxation of price control was always a little ahead of the relaxation of wage control. They could easily have been coordinated had the government taken care that that be done.
For instance, in January they relaxed the rule which prevented any wage increases except where there was gross injustice and inequality, in favour of the rule allowing increases only to equalize rates in an area. At the same time in January the government had the recommendations of the Canadian Congress of Labour, of which Mr. Pat Conroy is secretary, that that second stage should have been relaxed and that the rule of "just and reasonable within the price structure" should have been substituted for the existing regulation. The government should not have waited until the following June to do that.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext: If I may correct my hon. friend, the congress of labour wanted the abolition of wage control, the reinstatement of collective bargaining and the maintenance of price control. That is the record.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
I have the record here of Mr. Conroy's evidence, and I refer to page 754 of the proceedings. He states that in January, in response to a request by the minister for his opinion, he recommended:
*1. There should be .a free range for negotiation between employers and unions of at least ten cents an hour, with a further proviso that, where reduction in hours of work is agreed upon, or has been effected, provision should be made for a larger amount than ten cents an hour.

Industrial Relations .
The national and regional war labour boards should have authority to increase wages to such levels as are deemed fair and reasonable, thus eliminating the provision "for the same or comparable work in the same or similar localities." In short, in order to meet the need of constant production and of a high living standard the use of obscure language and equally obscure interpretations should be discontinued.
Those were the two recommendations made by the congress. They were not followed by the government, although the government had asked the congress for its opinion.

I am referring to the January incident, not to April.
There seem to have been three times at which there could have been a settlement of these problems, and the government, by failing to seize the opportunity, failed so to settle. One was in January, one in April, and one was at the time of the appointment of the controller.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour

speechtext: Let us have the April one.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
I am referring at the moment to January. In January, at the time Mr. Conroy made these recommendations to the government, he made this extraordinary prophecy-extraordinary	in its accuracy,
judged by later events. He wrote a letter from which I quote two paragraphs. He said:
The foregoing are the minimum that labour can subscribe to in the present transitional period. We believe that, in view of the existing situation in the United States and the expected impact of the results of the same in this country, wisdom should dictate a liberal and orderly process of transition rather than the amendment of the regulations -within narrow limits, which would undoubtedly be unsatisfactory and open the gate to a deluge of wage controversies and possible dislocation throughout the country. It may be said that, having started in the United States, the deluge may be beyond us in any event, and therefore why bother about an orderly transition? This would seem to us to be specious reasoning, and its only effect would be a partial halt to reconversion, with continued shortages of goods and the inevitable breaking down of resistance to maintaining an economic price level.
And then these significant words:
The question to be considered is whether we should move in advance of the heavy impact of these situations or wait until we cannot control them.
So that there it was quite apparent that so far as this congress, which is the congress particularly affected, is concerned, had that ten-cent increase or the power to grant the
ten-cent increase been given in January, it would have satisfied Mr. Conroy and his congress.
Then we come to April, when we had it in evidence that ten cents offered then would probably have sw'Rled the steel strike.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext: Then we come to the last chance of averting the strike, which was when the controller was appointed. Just before the controller was appointed, we had evidence that the Minister of Labour knew that the union was not prepared to accept ten cents, and yet the appointment of the controller was coupled with what I call the ten-cent speech or the ten-cent letter which the minister read in April.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
Well, it is the telegram. But it seems to me that at that time, had the controller been put in and no ten-cent limit imposed by indirection, this strike against the controller might never have taken place. It seems to me that when you couple that with the government's lack of resolution in dealing with the strike incident when it did arise, you have a very serious failure in the administration of labour policy. When the strike threatened the government passed this order in council; it contained penalties in the event of breach, and when the strike took place in defiance of the order in council it became apparent that the government of Canada was bluffing; and I say to you in all seriousness, Mr. Speaker, I do not believe the government of Canada should ever bluff.
Much has been said about lawlessness on the part of these unions, and I join with the minister in condemning it utterly. I do not believe there is any situation in Canada where any citizen is entitled to .break the law; and when I say that, I mean the law as it stands, and not the law as some people want it to be. But I say that there is such a thing as leading a person up to greater and greater breaches of the law, by undue laxity and leniency in the inception of the difficulty. This trouble started in about 1943, when unions of this congress first showed that they
Industrial Relations

did not wish to'follow the machinery of the regional war labour board, and they got part of their demands even though they behaved in an illegal fashion. Then we had illegality on the picket lines across this country last winter and more and more so this summer. No action was taken, and finally we come up to the time when the order in council is passed, when bodies in the country feel strong enough, or feel the government is weak enough, to disobey the order of the government appointing the controller and saying that they should stay at work. I do not think we can blame all the lawlessness on labour when we have a situation like that. They were fighting for what they thought was right; they were just edging along and seeing what they could get away with; they got away with too much, and the responsibility for that is on the government.
I believe that this steel strike is not a problem only in labour-management relations. I do not believe, although in the main it is a strike against the steel companies, it is entirely that. I think it is also a strike against the government's wage control policy. For the solution of this strike and for the solution of the labour crisis which we are going through I do not think we need at this moment any new labour law, although I hope improvements will result very shortly. But I believe a solution of our present difficulties requires only the exercise by the government of its two responsibilities; first, its responsibility to maintain price and wage control in, order to prevent inflation, and1, second, its responsibility to maintain law and order in the country. If it does both those things in the interests, not of labour and management or any particular party, but of the Canadian people as a whole, and applies those principles and follows them to their logical conclusion, the steel strike will be solved), as will all labour unrest in, the country.
I just want to refer to that responsibility which the government has for price and wage control in Canada, and particularly to show what is happening out in my part of the country, in British Columbia. It was there that the first fifteen-cent settlement was reached, and that may have precipitated the difficulties which we now face. But the government has never said that there is a ten-cent ceiling in this country. They have rather put up Mr. Gordon, who says that, or something approximating to it; but every time we pressed the ministers to say whether ten cents was government policy they said "No, we will not say what government policy is; the regional war labour boards are entirely autonomous, and we are not going to inter-

fere with what they do." What happened out in British Columbia? First of all, there was a fifteen-cent settlement in lumber, and after that, some forty or more settlements between management and labour, joint settlements and joint applications to the board for approval of wage increases of fifteen to seventeen cents. Although the minister never, as a matter of government policy, supported Donald Gordon in, his ten-cent statement, the board out in British Columbia did not feel itself quite as autonomous as the minister seems to think it was. After Mr. Gordon's statement, the board out there imposed an interim ten-cent ceiling pending instructions from Ottawa, and Mr. Pearson, the minister of labour of British Columbia, and the chairman of the board, is reported as follows:
He disclosed that he had asked Ottawa for specific directions on whj' the increase above ten cents would be disastrous to the national economy and he said that pending clarification from Ottawa the ten-cent limit "is the only-reasonable thing we can do. After all, we are only a junior board and we must take our direction from the federal authorities on a matter of this kind."
While the minister is saying that the board is autonomous, the board is saying that it is not autonomous and wants instructions. After that, the minister, according to press reports, gave an answer to the board in which he said that:
. . . the department had given no instructions to the B.C. war labour board to limit increases to ten cents an hour. He suggested that the B.C. Board might have decided to withhold final decision on cases until it saw what action would be taken by the commons industrial relations committee which is investigating the whole situation.
Following that denial, as I call it, of Donald Gordon, the British Columbia regional war labour board announced that it was going to deal with each case on its merits and without relationship to Donald Gordon's statement. Unfortunately, I have not yet got the paper of last Friday which contains that statement and I do not know exactly what Mr. Pearson said, but that is the sense of it. So that we now have this situation. In British Columbia fifteen cents has been granted. Forty applications for fifteen cents still exist; forty applications for fifteen cents will probably be passed by the British Columbia board, and a pattern of fifteen cents will be set in British Columbia. But the minister says that his personal view is that Donald, Gordon is right and that ten cents will break the price ceiling and that we cannot have more than ten cents in eastern Canada.
Surely the government has to do one of two things. It has to come out and support Mr. Gordon's statement, or else it must repudiate

Industrial Relations
Mr. Gordon's statement. The government cannot support it in eastern Canada and repudiate it in the west, because British Columbians probably just as much as anyone else, care whether price control is maintained. In my view, therefore, it is absolutely essential, not only for the settlement of the steel strike, but also for the solution of the wider difficulty, that the government give an authoritative statement on what our economy will stand, and so persuade all parties to get in behind them and support them in the position they take in the interests of the whole country.
The last thing I wish to say is that we must have a government which will administer the law fearlessly and without hesitation or equivocation. I do not believe there is any class of persons or any person in this country who can defy our law, and if the law is not suited to what we want, then this is the place in which to change it. But at any moment we have certain laws standing on the statute books. It is the responsibility of the government to enforce that law as it stands I am quite sure that when all the people of Canada know that the government will enforce the law as it is laid1 down by parliament, we shall quickly get rid of this lawlessness, this bypassing of boards, or violence on the picket line which has contributed so much to bad labour relations in the country.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
I should like to make a few observations, not in a critical sense but rather by way of appreciation of the opportunity that was mine to sit with the labour relations committee and study and seek to give some sense of direction to the government in one of the most critical moments in Canada's history. I shall always remember my experience in that committee. It was an opportunity to gain first-hand knowledge of the tremendous problems faced not only by the government but by the people of Canada. Of course the house is aware that the majority of the members of the committee were Liberals and supporters of the administration, but I hasten to say that I was never at any time conscious of that fact. There existed the best of good feeling and a sincere desire on the part of all to obtain all the evidence we could and to arrive at reasonable conclusions.
I was greatly impressed with the most magnificent presentation this afternoon by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith), and I say with him in effect that it is all very well for those who are outside, not charged with responsibility, to be critical of the report which the committee saw fit to return to the House of Commons. But we had to strike some balance, and we were not going to bring 63260-323
about that sense of confidence, or the possibility of solving our great problems, by indicating to one and all that we were biased in our views. I am sure that, as the various witnesses appeared before the committee, we became more and more convinced of the sincerity of those who came before us, and indeed they had a grasp of their problem and were able to convey a great deal of their knowledge to the committee.
I wish to refer for a moment to a brief sent to me by the Owen Sound board of trade. Unfortunately, it did not arrive in time to be presented to the committee, and I do not propose to read it in its entirety at the moment, but rather to say that the Owen Sound board of trade is comprised of 300 representative business and professional men of the community who sought to make a study in an approach to this great problem. Their representations to me are based in the main on this view, not to forget the great consuming public. I believe it was Mr. Conroy who said, in answer to a question, that his organization would probably represent between 300,000 and
350,000	people in Canada. That leaves a vast army amounting to millions who are not organized and who are now victims of the situation which confronts the country at the moment.
Therefore, in referring to the brief presented by the Owen Sound board of trade, I simply suggest to the government that we must not in any sense lose sight of the vast impact upon a multitude of people who can easily become the innocent victims of a policy which might lead us nowhere. I think it was with that thought in mind that I had some appreciation of the representations made by Mr. Donald Gordon. The committee were sincere in their report. We believed that price control could not be maintained without a measure of wage stabilization. Even though, in all sincerity, we might be inclined to question the judgment of one whose experience and background are sufficient to recommend him to any committee of parliament, nevertheless I do not think there was one member on the committee prepared to assume the awful responsibility of saying that he was wrong. I do say this and my observation was made to the committee, and I repeat it in effect now-that we have arrived at a time where price control cannot be held in rigidity; that there should be a degree of elasticity. In order to gain the cooperation of the Canadian people-and in my opinion if wTe are to maintain price ceilings or price control it will require the complete cooperation and self-discipline of the Canadian people-it must be brought home to them that in order to maintain price control the wartime

Industrial Relations

prices and trade board may have to retreat to a new line. In other words, these increases in prices, which would accompany an increase in wages, would be made more gradual to lighten the shock upon the economy; because it does seem to me that sooner or later we are going to reach a certain peak before we have accomplished that economy of plenty which we all believe will solve the problem of price control.
So far as the unions are concerned, I share the view that much of the agitation and much of the unrest apparent come from a source which is foreign to our Canadian democracy. I used words in committee to this effect, that the unions should seek to smoke out the communists, and I received the prompt reply that if they were to smoke out the communists there were a lot of others who should be smoked out as well. I can appreciate that it is not an easy problem; in fact it is a difficult one; but I have such a high regard for labour unions, and I feel that they are so necessary in an organized economy or in an organized society, that I hope they will continue to resist with all their efforts the inroads of communism and communistic doctrine. That is one thing which makes it more difficult to enforce the law and order to which the hon. member who has just taken his seat referred.
I am one of those who believe that every citizen in Canada who enjoys the protection which our laws provide should be prepared to accept his responsibility as a citizen and conform with those laws. The time has come when the government will have to give some evidence of their determination to see that law and order are respected in the country. That brings me to section 7 of the report which has not been touched upon particularly, and which reads as follows:
Your committee recommends that the controllers appointed by order in council P.C. 2904 be instructed to implement the terms of such order with such modifications as the government may determine.
I believe there is a possibility of some misunderstanding of this section. That is apparent particularly in some editorial comments in regard to these words "with such modifications as the government may determine". I think the spirit and the understanding of the committee was that if it were necessary to strengthen the controllers' hands it should be done. There was no intention of giving direction to the government to restrict the controllers. I take clause 7 to mean that, if necessary, the government would be prepared to strengthen the controller's hands to see that his administration was admitted and that every effort would be made to return men to work and production started and maintained.

I can well remember that evening almost a month ago when we started out with such high hopes for the accomplishments of the committee. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) outlined the nature of our inquiry. He expressed the hope that farmers, consumers and others would be heard, along with those who have been heard by the committee. I believe that it was only' the time factor which caused us not to interview farmers and those who might be considered organized consumers. It was for that reason that I recommended or sought to have included in the report a resolution to state that this committee should be reconvened at the earliest possible moment at the next session of parliament. I understand that I would be in order in making a motion of that kind at that time.
If I have any criticism at all to offer with regard to the government's attitude it is to the effect that this committee was not called into being at an earlier date. However, as someone has said, it is always easy to look backwards and criticize the government; but the government did know that the country was seething with industrial unrest. I join with the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) in what he has said. I am sure that every member of the committee agrees with him in saying that the deliberations of the committee justified its existence. Because of that fact, the government may not have realized early enough the contributon which the committee could have made. Had the committee been called together at an earlier date, it might have accomplished a great deal. Much remains to be done. Our Canadian economy will not permit of strikes. We are producers. At this very moment there is a possibility of Canada gaining access to markets which might be denied us in a very short time. That will react very badly on the nation's welfare. If we can play some part now and later in seeing that the proper formula is worked out, either in committee or by the government, which will provide for some stability of employment and remove this irritation and bring about some semblance of confidence in each other, then we can really get somewhere. I think it was Mr. Brockington who left the thought with the committee that long periods of strife and strikes lead to greater difficulties in settling disputes. That was in evidence in the committee. As the hon. member for Calgary West said this afternoon, it is certainly no tribute to the employers of labour when a leading industrialist in Canada has to admit that the first time he met the national directors and the bargaining agency of his factory was here in Ottawa, after the strike

Industrial Relations
had been in progress for many weeks. I am saying that, not entirely in a spirit of criticism, but in the hope that better understanding and greater confidence in each other will bring about better relations between management and workers. As we grow to nationhood, as our great industrial machine expands and industries become so huge that thousands are employed, the old personal touch is gone. Yet by the same token I think we must all recognize that it would be impossible to bargain with each one individually, as might have been the' case when the industries were of smaller proportions. So it would seem that for many years to come there will have to be some bargaining agency, and I believe the sooner industry recognizes that fact, the better it will be.
I want now to say a word in reply to the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), and I also made this observation in the committee. He was asked this question, and I did not get his answer: Would he be prepared to subsidize all industry in Canada? That is a fair question which requires some consideration. I have only to remind hon. members that, after all, subsidies come out of taxes, and that taxes come out of the pockets of the people and enter into the cost of production of our manufacturers. Oitr costs of production can have a great effect on our ability to secure our share of the export markets of the world. The time is not far distance when competition in world trade will be a vital factor, and we should always keep that thought in mind if we are to guarantee employment to Canadian workers. Reference has been made to our tremendous contribution to the war effort, which we may all applaud and greatly admire. But one factor is often overlooked. It will also be found in the record that we borrowed about $13,500 million of the $25,000 or $27,000 million we spent on account of the war, and we still have that money to repay. If we continue to indulge in subsidies, at a time when collectively we probably have more money than we ever had before, then the outlook for the future is bad. I think the time for the government to do its pump-priming, if it has to use subsidies, is when private enterprise fails to take up the slack, not when we are moving into a cycle of expansion and greater prosperity. As a matter of fact I think economists will agree that to-day we have more money collectively than we ever had before. In 1939 I believe we had something like $281 per capita. We now have something over $1,000 per capita; and we have over $6,250 million in liquid resources. If I were to remind hon. members that we financed our 1929 disaster on about 82,300 million of liquid 63260-3231
resources they will understand the tremendous task which faces those charged with the responsibility of maintaining the price ceiling, .while this huge volume of money is seeking an outlet on a market which is still short of supplies and will remain short for some time to come. The danger will become greater unless we step up production to meet demand, and we shall not step up that production as long as there are strikes and industries are closing down. It can lead to grave disaster; the moment is critical indeed.
That is one thought which encourages me to say I believe there must be greater elasticity in the price ceiling, so that the controller may retreat to a new line and bring home a clear picture to the Canadian public in order that they may realize that if costs of production are to increase, so will the cost of living increase. But I cannot believe that the danger in regard to the price ceiling will be any greater than it will become very shortly if we continue to have lack of production, with our workers idle and our industries closed down. We hear about new money, or social credit, or whatever it may be called, I know our difficulty at the present time is to encourage people to work for the money we are now offering. If we are to hand out money without any work at all I do not know whether I shall be able to get anyone to cook my meals for me. I would be afraid we were living too close to what is very easy to achieve, a currency that is not worth a great deal. In other worda, the value of money depends entirely upon its acceptability and upon general confidence in the government of a country.
I want to dwell just for a moment on a statement made by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) and the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) with respect to recommendation No. 6. The only observation I have to make is that I do not see how we are depriving anyone of anything if we supply them with ballots upon which they can exercise their own good judgment, untrammelled and unafraid, because I feel sure that a vote taken under government supervision would show exactly what the workers most desired.
This afternoon there seemed to be doubt in the minds of some as to what the deputy minister, through the minister, said with respect to the war labour board, and I want to read from page 406 of the proceedings of the committee. I shall read the complete paragraph. This is Mr. MacNamara's sworn testimony:
On June 27, during the morning, the minister, deputy minister and director of industrial relations met with Mr. Murray Cotterill. The minister reviewed the general situation in Canada and expressed the opinion that the general
Industrial Relations

pattern of wage increase should not exceed 10 cents per hour. In the afternoon the deputy mimster made a proposal to Mr. Cotterill that the department, under a plan in mind, could arrange for the appropriate regional war labour boards to issue a directive for a rate increase equal to 10 cents per hour, the increase to be worked out in a manner found desirable and reasonable by the union. One method suggested was that an increase of 8 cents per hour be granted all around, and in addition that overtime rates of time and one-half be paid after 44 hours per week on the understanding that the plants would operate 48 hours per week for the present. The deputy minister gave a firm commitment that he would request the wage boards to issue the directive and also that, if an appeal was taken to the national board, he was quite convinced the latter would not upset the decision.
We had considerable questioning in the committee on that very point, because it left the impression that the boards were not entirely independent- bodies. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt) has said, they were not autonomous bodies; they were bound to a government policy, which the ministers who were examined refused to admit was government policy; and I believe that, has led to much of the difficulty that exists at the present time.
I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that my experiences while serving on the committee will be lasting. We were given the greatest latitude, and I think the very fact that when Mr. Brockington was recommended as mediator the government immediately acted upon that suggestion. He was appointed and, before we concluded our deliberations, was able to bring us a comprehensive report which indicated his faithfulness. His fine work in endeavouring to bring the parties together, though without success, did impress upon us the feeling that in this instance a parliamentary committee did mean something-we were not hampered in any way in our undertakings; the members of the committee expressed themselves freely, and there were many surprises. If we could just carry forward a few steps the spirit shown there, I believe that, through the education the public received as a result of the sittings of the committee being held in public and the amount of publicity those proceedings were given, we may be able to get somewhere in dealing with our problems; and to that end I promise the ministry my wholehearted support.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I, at the outset, tender to the chairman of the industrial relations committee (Mr. Lalonde) using his mother tongue which is also mine, my heartiest congratulations for the efficiency and the ability he has displayed in directingi the discussions of that committee. We have especially

noted the dignity with which he has discharged that important duty, his courtesy toward the numerous witnesses who have appeared before the committee, and toward the members of that body. He has always shown absolute impartiality and the aptness of the rulings he had to give on -matters of procedure, in -the course of our discussions, has always evidenced an enlightened legal mind.
I was especially honoured in being invited to second the motion he has moved, Mr. Speaker, for concurrence in this report. It is quite a substantial report which will certainly command the attention of all friends of labour and will have much influence on the progressive development of relations between employers and workers.
(Text): Mr. Speaker, as the seconder of the motion now before the house, I believe it is fitting that I make a few comments in the debate, even though previous speakers have, in my view, already covered the subject matter of this discussion pretty well. I had the good fortune of -being in -the chamber to listen to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) and to the hon. member for Calgary West'(Mr. Smith). I feel that they have given an accurate and complete summary of the proceedings which took place, and that they have interpreted to the house the meaning of the recommendations now placed before hon. members.
I wish at this point to join with previous speakers in congratulating the chairman of the committee. He has been regular in the discharge of his high function, and has done it in a most impartial and able way.
I wish also to take this opportunity to thank those responsible for my appointment to this important committee. In the past I had scarcely had an opportunity to go so deeply into labour relations. This opportunity comes at what I consider a serious hour in our programme of reconversion from war to peace-time production.
When the committee began its sittings a controller had already been appointed for some days, and had taken over the management of the plants involved in the dispute. The country was anxious about the dispute in this, its most important basic industry, and about a strike which was to affect so deeply general production in other fields of our activities.
Under its terms of reference the committee had to investigate generally the causes of industrial unrest in the country, so that it might report its findings and conclusions to the house. It held forty-eight sittings, during which time it did a magnificent job. If I

Industrial Relations
were to compare the work of the industrial relations committee with that of any other committee in this or any other previous session, I would say that in the same period of time there has been no committee in the past which achieved such important results as did the committee on industrial relations.
As I said at the outset, my interest in the work of the committee comes from the fact that in the past I had not had an opportunity to go very deeply into the causes of any industrial unrest. My attendance in the committee gave me a better knowledge of what trade unionism means, its purpose and its necessity. I am convinced more than ever that trade unionism, in a democracy such as the one in which we live, is a true expression of the natural development of labour. It is an expansion of the individual rights which may be developed in smaller circles such as the family, or in other larger social or religious groups, and which find their natural development in trade unionism or professional associations.
The process of forming unions is certainly to be encouraged. It has to be developed, so long as that development follows the lines of true democracy In a democracy the basis of all our activities and the reason for our legislation is that of safeguarding and developing the rights of the individual. Our legislation must also protect the individual in all his fields of activity, and must therefore, in matters relating to labour, give a hand in the development of trade unionism. Otherwise, as obtains in a dictatorship, trade unions do not represent the natural expansion of individual rights, but become the instrument of the state to impose its doctrine and its policies of action upon the worker, whereas the opposite should be done in a democracy.
Therefore I believe strongly in trade unions. When I look at the achievements they have attained in the past, the increased standard of living they have provided1 the worker, the increase in his security, I consider that so long as democracy is present, and so long as such principles are developed in trade unions, we shall march forward toward real progress.
In some circles there is a wrong impression prevailing with regard to trade unions. In my opinion the cause for this is the fact that too much emphasis, too much publicity has been given to the difficult phases of the relations between labour and management. Not enough effort has been made to keep the country informed as to what trade unions have really done. When we have a strike we must not forget that there are hundreds of incidents between companies and unions which have
been satisfactorily settled in a friendly way. In the private life of an individual it is said that happiness does not make history, and I think the same is true of trade unions. We hear too much about their failures to achieve their end and we do not hear enough about what they have really lone. During the war which has just concluded, the membership of trade unions in Canada increased from around
200,000	until it is now on its way to attain the million mark. We all know, from our experience in our own parts of the country, of the improvements which have been brought about in the lot of the worker by the activities of trade unions.
The committee made seven specific recommendations to this house, six of which I think have already received the approval of members of the committee and, I am sure, of the members of this chamber. I should like to offer a few comments on two of the recommendations which I consider to be of the utmost importance. The first recommendation in the report to which I should like to refer is recommendation No. 6 which provides for a strike vote to be taken at the request of one of the parties concerned and at the discretion of the minister. I have examined this recommendation and have come to the conclusion that it affords a safeguard to both parties to an industrial dispute. I cannot understand the views of those who oppose this recommendation. I see in it two guarantees. First, one of the parties must take the responsibility before the other party and the country generally of having a strike vote taken. In the second place, the minister must exercise bis discretion; he must decide whether the request for a strike vote should be granted.
In my judgment, this recommendation should commend itself to the workers, first, because it provides labour with an opportunity to be sure that its will will be taken into account when industrial relations have reached a certain stage. It has been said, particularly of new organizations-and I think this would apply to most trade union locals in Canada- that the direction is too often in the hands of inexperienced men or of a radical element. That is only natural in the development of trade unionism. This recommendation should do much to give a certain amount of assurance to the worker that when the critical hour comes in his relations with management he will have a say in the final decision to be taken.
The unions should not have any objection to this clause. I feel it will strengthen their position. If they give gmd leadership to
